title: The Fathers on Luke
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The angel stood at the altar of incense, which lay inside, so Zechariah was in the Holy of Holies.
comments.comment: “And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense” (Luke 1:11). He did not say “the altar of sacrifices,” but “the altar of incense.” For the outer altar was for sacrifices and burnt offerings, but the inner one was for incense. So from this, and from the fact that the angel appeared to him alone, and from the statement that the people were outside waiting for him, it is quite clear that he entered the Holy of Holies.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse names the altar of incense and where Zechariah stood.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Mary was of David's house, since she went to Bethlehem and the text says the virgin was of that house.
comments.comment: From this it is clear to us that the Virgin also is of Davidic descent; for since she was from Bethlehem, it is obvious that she was also of the house and lineage of David. … For Joseph's genealogy was traced, but no one enumerated her ancestors the way they did his. So that you may not doubt and say, "How then is it clear that she too is from David?" listen: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David (Luke 1:26-27). The phrase "of the house of David" must be understood as spoken about the Virgin;
comments.selected_reason: Answers a reader's question whether Mary, and not only Joseph, was of David's line.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: The Lord who is with Mary is no earthly bridegroom but the Maker himself, who comes from her.
comments.comment: Therefore with those words, Hail, full of grace, the Angel first greeted her and addressed her: The Lord is with you (Luke 1:28). Not an earthly bridegroom, but the Lord of holiness Himself, the father of chastity, the author of incorruption and the giver of freedom; the one who brings about salvation, and the keeper and giver of true peace; who created man from the virgin earth (Genesis 2:7), and took Eve from his side and rib (Genesis 2:21-22): this Lord is with you, and in turn comes from you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the Lord is with you' means in this greeting.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Mary was troubled by the greeting because she had resolved to keep her virginity.
comments.comment: Beautiful is the angel's greeting to her who is above the angels, for it brings joy to the whole world. But she was troubled at the word (Luke 1:29), for she was not used to speaking with men; she had firmly resolved to keep her virginity.
comments.selected_reason: Says why Mary was troubled at the greeting.
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: The angel comes to take away the cause of fear, and grace is not to be measured by the laws of nature.
comments.comment: And do not fear, Mary: for I have not come to strike fear into you, but to drive the cause of fear away from you. Do not fear, Mary; for you have found grace with God (Luke 1:30). Do not judge grace by the measure of nature; for grace does not allow itself to be made subject to the laws of nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the angel says 'do not be afraid' and what finding grace implies.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Mary found grace because she was worthy of it, keeping soul and body virgin, and the name Jesus means Saviour.
comments.comment: Truly she found grace, she who was worthy of grace. She found grace who had tilled the labours of grace and reaped a rich harvest. She found grace who brought forth the seeds of grace and reaped the full-flowing harvest of grace. She found a depth of grace, she who kept safe and whole the ship of her twofold virginity: for she kept her soul a virgin no less than her body, and that is why the virginity of her body was also kept. “And you will bear a son,” he says, “and you shall call his name Jesus” (Luke 1:31). Jesus means Saviour, “for he will save his people from their iniquities” (Matthew 1:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Mary 'found grace' and gives the meaning of the name Jesus.
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: Gabriel's announcement began joy for Mary and ended for women the pain and sadness that followed the first virgin's transgression.
comments.comment: The archangel Gabriel was the first to cry out to her, saying 'Rejoice, favored one, the Lord is with you; behold, you will conceive in the womb and give birth to a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel' (Luke 1:31). This announcement was the beginning of joy for her, as it removed the painful consequences of the first virgin's transgression, which had enclosed all women in pain and bitterness. Through Gabriel's gospel, the second virgin stopped every source of pain in childbirth and scattered the cloud of sadness in childbearing, surrounding her fellow women with the lights of joy.
comments.selected_reason: Shows why the announcement is called good news, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: Homily II on Saint Mary the Mother of God

comments.capsule: Mary asked how she could conceive while remaining a virgin, and the angel answered that the child would be called Son of God, because he is what he is called.
comments.comment: Then Mary said to the Angel: How will this be done to me, since I do not know a man? (Luke 1:34) Shall I still remain a virgin? Will the dignity of virginity in me be betrayed and lost? While the most holy Virgin, as if in wonder, was turning these things over in her mind, the Angel briefly sets out the sum of his message and says: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. And therefore the holy one who will be born of you will also be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). For what He is, that He will also surely be called. Fittingly, then, grace chose holy Mary alone out of all generations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Mary's question and the angel's answer in plain terms.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Mary's question was a plea to know the manner of a conception beyond nature, and the Creator of nature changes its boundaries by his own authority.
comments.comment: And what does the treasure of true wisdom say to this? She does not imitate Eve, her first mother; rather, she sets right Eve's carelessness, and calls on nature as her advocate, arguing against the angel's word in some such way as this: “How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34). “You speak of impossible things,” she says. “Your word breaks the boundaries of nature that the One who fashioned it set in place. I will not bear to be called a second Eve and to cheat the will of the Maker. But if what you say is not against God, tell me the manner of the conception and resolve my doubt.” To her the angel of truth replies: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). What is being done here is no slave to the laws of nature. For the Creator and Master of nature changes the boundaries of nature by his own authority.
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: Since the child is called the Son of God, he is God, equal in glory with the Father.
comments.comment: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born of you will also be called the Son of God (Luke 1:35). But if He is the Son of God, He is also God, of the same form as the Father and coeternal with Him. In Him the Father possesses all glory; He is, in His own person, the imprint and the image, and through the radiance the glory shines out (Hebrews 1:3).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Mary alone received the mysteries hidden from patriarchs and prophets, and where grace is present all things are possible with God.
comments.comment: You know, Mary, what was hidden from the patriarchs and prophets. You have learned, O Virgin, what until now was hidden even from the angels. You have heard, most holy one, what the choir of those inspired by the divine Spirit was never found worthy to hear. Moses and David, Isaiah and Daniel, and all the prophets foretold Him, but they did not know the manner or the reason. But you alone, most holy Virgin, now receive the mysteries that were unknown to all of them, and you understand their cause. For where the Holy Spirit is, all things are brought to completion readily and without delay. Where divine grace is present, all things are possible with God (Luke 1:37; Matthew 19:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why 'nothing is impossible with God' is said to Mary.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Only God can give the gift of prophecy, so the child leaping at Mary's greeting shows that the one she carried is God.
comments.comment: When God works the gift of prophecy, someone becomes a prophet; in any other way, not at all. So when the greeting of the holy virgin Mary, still carrying Jesus, moved John in the womb into prophecy, how is Christ not God — who even in the virgin’s womb moved the Baptist in a God-befitting way into the power of prophecy?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the child leaped in Elizabeth's womb.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The fruit of Mary's womb is not from a man's seed but from the Holy Spirit, unlike the fruit of David's loins.
comments.comment: For it is said to her by Elizabeth, 'Blessed is the fruit of your womb' (Luke 1:42). And 'fruit of the womb' is the name for that which is not from a man, but from Mary alone, through the Holy Spirit having come upon her and the power of the Most High having overshadowed her. For those who have received seed from the fathers are those fruits; for it is said to David, 'From the fruit of your loins I will set someone upon your throne' (2 Sam 7:12), teaching him that his kingdom shall not fail like that of Saul, but that this shall be directed from his succession.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase 'fruit of your womb'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Magnifying the Lord adds nothing to God; it adds to the one who magnifies, who shares in his greatness.
comments.comment: Just as magnifying God does not imply adding greatness to Him, nor does glorifying Him imply bringing fame to Him from without, so neither does sanctifying the Lord mean adding holiness to Him; … he who magnifies Him receives a participation in His own greatness; whence it is said: 'my soul magnifies the Lord' (Luke 1:46)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that a soul 'magnifies' the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mary's blessedness came not from her death but from the conception itself, as she said all generations would call her blessed.
comments.comment: For your blessedness is not your death; your passing did not become your perfecting, nor does your departure bestow your security. For in your case the beginning, the middle and the end of all the good things that pass understanding, and their security and true confirmation, were the conception without seed, the divine indwelling and the birth without corruption. That is why you truly said that you would be called blessed by all generations (Luke 1:48), not from your death but from the conception itself.
comments.author: John of Damascus
comments.work: Homilies on the Dormition of the Mother of God

comments.capsule: A horn of salvation means a king of salvation, since Scripture calls kings horns.
comments.comment: Regarding God, he says this: 'A horn of salvation has arisen for us from the house of David' (Luke 1:69), which is to say, a king of salvation. For in many places of the Scripture, and not at all least in the wise Daniel, kings and queens are called horns.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the figure of the 'horn of salvation'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is the dawn from on high who brings us out of darkness and death into life and light in the Lord.
comments.comment: This man shown by the prophet is called a dawn, concerning which in the Gospel Zechariah, the father of the Baptist, having been filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke out: 'A dawn from on high has appeared to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death' (Luke 1:78), in order that, the darkness being released and the shadow of death no longer existing, we might pass from death into life, and having shone forth, we might become light in the Lord, casting away the darkness of the ignorance of God and of the rest of evil, we might become light in the Lord according to the philosophy of those writing: 'For you were darkness, but now light in the Lord' (Ephesians 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the dawn image in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Evangelist names the census to fix the day of Christ's birth and to show God's plan, since God moved Augustus to issue the decree so that even unwillingly he served the coming of the Only-Begotten.
comments.comment: … From this it is clear that He was born at the time of the first census. And anyone who wishes can consult the ancient public records in Rome, learn the time of the census, and know it precisely. … The Evangelist did not mark this time without purpose, but to make the day clear and known to us, and to reveal God's plan of salvation. For Augustus did not issue that decree on his own or from himself, but God moved his soul, so that even unwillingly he might serve the coming of the Only-Begotten.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Luke dates the birth by the census, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Christ had to be born in Bethlehem as the prophets said, so the registration law drove Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to that city, God arranging his plan of salvation in this way.
comments.comment: … All the prophets foretold that Christ would come not from Nazareth, but from Bethlehem, and would be born there. For it is written: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for out of you shall come a ruler who will shepherd my people Israel” (Micah 5:2). … Since Joseph and Mary were citizens of Bethlehem, but leaving that city they had established their life in Nazareth and were staying there—as indeed often happens with many people, who leave the cities where they were born and spend their time in other cities where they were not originally from—and since Christ had to be born in Bethlehem, the decree went out, pushing them even unwillingly into that city, God arranging the plan of salvation in this way. For the law commanding each person to register in his own fatherland forced them to rise from there—I mean from Nazareth—and come to Bethlehem to register. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Joseph and Mary went to Bethlehem, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: He was laid in a manger because crowds had already filled all the places.
comments.comment: … For as soon as they set foot in the city, Jesus was immediately born. Therefore he was also laid in a manger, since many people were rushing together from everywhere at that time, occupying the places beforehand and causing great crowding. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain reason for the manger.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Calling Christ her firstborn does not mean other sons followed, for the Only-begotten Word is named firstborn because he shared our flesh and blood and became firstborn among many brothers.
comments.comment: … The holy virgin has borne one and only son, Emmanuel. How then does it say “her son, the firstborn” (Luke 2:7)? For others have not come to be after him, and she has remained a virgin. So it is marked from the God-breathed scripture: the Only-begotten Word of God has been named firstborn. For he has shared blood and flesh and similarly to us shared the same things. Thus he became firstborn among many brothers; yet as God he is worshiped by us ourselves and by the spirits above. …
comments.selected_reason: Answers a common question about the word 'firstborn' in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The Maker of all had no place, for he chose the utmost lowliness for our sake.
comments.comment: And there was not even room for them in the inn (Luke 2:7). He who built heaven and earth by His word (Genesis 1:1) had no place. For though He was rich, for our sake He became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), choosing the utmost lowliness for the salvation of our nature, out of the goodness toward us that is His by nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of 'no room' for the Maker of all.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The cave in Bethlehem and the manger in it are still shown, and even outsiders to the faith know that Jesus was born there.
comments.comment: … In keeping with the Gospel account of his birth, the cave in Bethlehem where he was born is shown, and the manger in the cave where he was wrapped in swaddling cloths (Luke 2:7). And what is shown there is widely known in those parts, even among those who are strangers to the faith: that in this cave was born the Jesus whom Christians worship and admire. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah's name for Christ, God with us, comes from his nature and his coming in the flesh, and the angel's name Savior comes from what he does, so the two do not clash.
comments.comment: … For the divine prophet, speaking mysteries in the Spirit, announced beforehand God made to be with us, giving Him this name from His nature and from His dispensation in the flesh. The blessed angel, for his part, gave Him the name from what He does; for He has saved His own people. That is why He has been called Savior. Indeed, when He underwent birth according to the flesh for our sake, the hosts of angels brought the shepherds the good news of the birth, saying: “Do not be afraid; for behold, we bring you good news today of a great joy, which is for all the people: today a Savior has been born, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10–11). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the angel's title differs from the prophet's name.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Choirs of angels surrounded Christ in the manger, which was a royal throne of the cherubim where he rested.
comments.comment: He who carried out the whole providence and ordering of the hidden mysteries of the dispensation, in heaven in the bosom of the Father and in the cave in His mother's arms, rested in the manger. Choirs of angels surrounded Him, singing glory in heaven and announcing peace on earth (Luke 2:13-14). In heaven He sat at the right hand of the Father; and in the manger He rested as upon the cherubim. Truly this too was a throne of the cherubim, a royal throne: the holy of holies, alone glorious upon earth, holier than the holy, in which Christ our God rested. …
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: At the birth of Jesus the heavenly host praised God, and the demons lost their strength and their sorcery was undone.
comments.comment: … It is likely, then, that at the birth of Jesus too, since “a multitude of the heavenly host,” as Luke recorded and as I believe, praised God and said, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men” (Luke 2:13–14), the demons for this reason lost their strength and grew weak. Their sorcery was exposed and their working undone; they were overthrown not only by the angels who visited the region around the earth because of the birth of Jesus, but also by the soul of Jesus and the Godhead in him. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The angels' words mean that the Son came through a body to extend heaven's glory to earth, to be glorified in those sanctified on earth too.
comments.comment: He [Christ] has sanctified all things both divinely and carnally. … Such also is that which is said by the angels: 'glory to God in the highest and on earth peace among men of good will' (Luke 2:14). Because of this, the Son of God came through a body, in order to extend the glory that is in heaven onto the earth, and to be glorified not only in the holy ones according to heaven, but also in those being sanctified according to the earth. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the angels' song as glory in heaven reaching to earth.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Because goodwill came to be in men, much peace prevailed, and glory came in the highest through the saved who ascend there.
comments.comment: … For having been born of the virgin, a multitude of the heavenly host cried out, 'Glory to God in the highest,' say, 'and peace on earth, in men goodwill' (Luke 2:14). For because of the goodwill having come into being in men, much peace prevailed, the enemies of all those on earth having been destroyed; but also glory has become in the highest, of the saved men having the ascent unto the highest. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Others born from barren wombs were called holy to the Lord, but Christ alone, born of a virgin without opening her gates, is holy of the holies and Lord of lords.
comments.comment: … For the wonderful Luke says concerning Christ, that when the days of their purification were fulfilled according to the law of Moses (Luke 2:22), he led Jesus into Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord, just as it has been written in the law of the Lord, that every male opening a womb shall be called holy to the Lord (Luke 2:23). Samuel and Isaac and Jacob and Joseph and others who were born from barrenness by hope and by opening the unfruitful wombs of mothers were called holy to the Lord; but Christ alone from a virgin, the only, the only-begotten, having been born and not having opened virgin gates, is not merely holy to the Lord, but holy of the holies and lord of lords and god of gods and firstborn of firstborns, ruler of rulers and king of kings; and he shall be called and believed and worshiped, and now in the temple shall be proclaimed by Simeon. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the law's 'every male opening a womb' holds more for Christ than for others.
comments.author: Cyril of Jerusalem
comments.work: Homily on the Presentation of the Lord

comments.capsule: Christ fulfilled the law as its lawgiver and left his mother's virginity intact, so that he is not only holy but excels the commandment in his birth.
comments.comment: But Christ, as we have said, fulfilled his own law as lawgiver above the law. For he did not open the gate of the virgin, but left it closed. He did not break the seal of nature, nor did he harm the one who bore him; he left intact for her the form of virginity. If you do not believe this, learn from Ezekiel: "And he turned me back along the way of the gate of the sanctuary of the outer court, the one facing east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: This gate shall remain closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, for the Lord, the God of Israel, shall enter and go out through it, and it shall remain closed" (Ezekiel 44:1-2). "Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord" (Luke 2:23). But this one is not only holy. As much as he surpasses in sanctification, so much does he also excel in birth and rise above the commandment of the law. …
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Luke left out the offering of the wealthy because he remembered the poor one who became poor for our sake, and he himself was the Lamb of God who offered himself for the world.
comments.comment: … Nevertheless, it says, "to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons" (Luke 2:24). Luke left the law incomplete, not seized by ignorance but guided by wisdom. The law said "a lamb and a young pigeon," but if the one offering could not afford it, it commanded "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons and fine flour." Luke, however, omitted the offering of the wealthy, for he remembered the poor one who willingly became poor for our sake. He had no lodging, it says; how could he have acquired a lamb? Wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger, how could he offer a sheep? Rather, he had no need of a lamb, for he himself was "the lamb of God" (John 1:29), the true sheep. He offered himself for the world. For this reason Luke declared what the law commanded, and signified what Christ was accomplishing. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Luke names only the poor offering.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Simeon's name means hearing of God, so it fits a man of obedience to the law who lives a good life, and his being a man in Jerusalem is a wonder.
comments.comment: … He was not only "a man," but he was also named Simeon. … "Behold, a man"—where? "In Jerusalem." The word carries astonishment; the phrase is full of wonder. A man in Jerusalem, about which the prophet Zephaniah introduced God himself saying: "I will search Jerusalem with a lamp and will not find a man" (Zephaniah 1:12). Does the light need a lamp? No, he says, but he calls the law a lamp. "And behold, a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon." And what is the interpretation of the name that is given? "Hearing of God." So he acquired a name befitting his way of life through the Spirit's dispensation. For where there is "hearing of God," there is certainly obedience to the law, keeping of commandments, the course of a good life, the goal of salvation drawing near to its end. In these things the true man is characterized, about whom these words were fittingly added. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of Simeon's name and of 'a man in Jerusalem'.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Simeon, with a pure body for the Spirit's dwelling, was promised that he would not see death before seeing the one who abolishes death.
comments.comment: … And 'there was a Holy Spirit upon him.' This is wonderful and appropriate also for those to whom it was spoken; for he had a temple, and his flesh had a pure bridal chamber, and he cleansed his soul of the entire worldly spider's web; from there he drew the Spirit's dwelling to himself. 'And he had been promised by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before seeing the Lord's Christ.' You see how great it is to be a temple of God; those who practice such a life pass from life to life. Therefore, to Simeon, 'it had been promised that he would not see death before seeing the Lord's Christ,' that is, before seeing the one who abolishes death, before seeing the one who raises the dead, before seeing the one who transforms tombs into a bridal chamber, before seeing the one who makes his departure from here fearless. …
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The promise meant passing from life to life, and Simeon, though neither priest nor Levite, could receive Christ because righteousness and devotion carry their own priesthood.
comments.comment: … So the revelation meant passing from life to life, journeying from light to light, leaping from day to day—not growing old, but being renewed, and receiving renewal at the time of the consummation. “He came in the Spirit into the temple” (Luke 2:27); the spring led the thirsty man to the spring. “And when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to what was customary, he himself received him into his arms” (Luke 2:27). In his hands he carried the One who holds the inhabited world and the uninhabited in his hand, “who measured the water in his hand and the heaven with a span and all the earth with his fist” (Isaiah 40:12). And how did Simeon offer a sacrifice that did not belong to him? For he was not a priest—that is not said—nor a Levite, nor a temple-keeper, since the liturgical office has been allotted to the tribe of Levi alone. He was not a priest, but he was “righteous,” and righteousness possesses the priesthood under its feet. He was not a Levite, but he was “devout,” and the devout man has the anointing from himself. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains Simeon's promise and why he could take the child in his arms.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Simeon is released because the time of forgiveness has come, a king is born who frees prisoners, and the peace he speaks of is that of the cross.
comments.comment: … And carrying the infant he said: “Now you release your servant, Master, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:29). “Now you release”—for the time of forgiveness had come, the ransom of the captives had arrived, the pardon of debts had come. A king was born who frees those in prisons, releases those in bonds, calls those in death back to life, and lightens the burden of the earth. “Now you release your servant, Master.” How do you know? I see the Master, he says, wearing the form of a servant. The Master would not have worn the form of a servant unless he had resolved to clothe the servant in the Master’s form. He would not have exchanged the order, nor would he who is high have been humbled, unless he had willed to lead the humble up to the height. But how do you “release him according to your word, in peace”? Simeon says: For if by a word you brought creation into being, by a word you certainly set free the ruler of creation. “In peace”—what peace? That of the cross. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Simeon means by being released in peace.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Simeon saw God in flesh, and the good things he brings are common to Jews and Gentiles, for the One who has come gives to all and takes from no one.
comments.comment: … I have seen what many longed to see and did not see: God in flesh, a sun shining in a cloud. “My eyes have seen your salvation,” that is, I have seen your incarnation, through which you arranged the salvation of humanity. For I did not see the bare Godhead, since no human being will see God as he is in essence. “Because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all the peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory for your people Israel” (Luke 2:31-32). The good things are common to Jews and Gentiles and undivided. So let the Jew not envy, let the Pharisee not be distressed, let the scribe not test, let Herod not fear for his kingdom, let Annas and Caiaphas not be afraid for their priesthood. The One who has come gives to all and takes from no one; he bestows generously, he grants without measure. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'your salvation' and 'light for the Gentiles' in plain terms.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: Christ is the stone of stumbling for those who disobey, while those who believe are not put to shame.
comments.comment: … “Behold, this one is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign spoken against.” (Luke 2:34) So the same one is the stone of stumbling and the rock of offense; and some, striking against him through disobedience, were shattered, while those who received the faith toward him escaped being put to shame. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The fall belongs to those who persist in unbelief and the rising to Christ, since those who fall through carelessness rise when they choose to.
comments.comment: And he says: “This child is set for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign of contradiction” (Luke 2:34)—for the fall of those who persist in unbelief, and for the rising of those who turn from unbelief to faith. Christ was a stone set for building, but the blind stumbled as their eyes wandered. So we must not attribute the fall of those who have fallen to him, but rather the rising. For if they only fell and did not also rise, you would rightly suspect him of causing the fall. But if those who fall through carelessness rise when they choose to, then the fall belongs to the careless one, and the rising belongs to Christ. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'the fall and rising of many' clearly.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The sign of contradiction is the cross, and the sword through Mary's soul was the doubt of many hearts about Christ at the passion, which shook even the chosen ones and his mother.
comments.comment: … The sign of contradiction is the cross. For when the Jews crucified him, the sun withdrew; the synagogue slandered him, and the earth shook. The crowd cried out, “Crucify him” (Luke 23:21), but the rocks, unable to bear the weight of the blasphemy, split apart. … “And a sword will pierce your own soul also, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). The sword is called division of mind, because just as a sword cuts and divides bodies, so division of mind leads souls to doubt. For even if she was a virgin, she was also a woman; even if she was the Mother of God, she was from our own clay. So the sword passed through her soul, “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35). What thoughts? The various thoughts about Christ at the time of the passion—sometimes calling him a prophet, sometimes not acknowledging him as the redeemer of Israel—and enduring great doubt about these things because of the turmoil of the passion. So the disciples with Cleopas came up and said to him, “Are you the only one staying in Jerusalem who does not know what has happened there in these days?” (Luke 24:18). Then, when asked “What things?”, they went on: “The things about Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet,” and so on (Luke 24:19). So they held him as a prophet and as the one who redeems Israel; but because of the passion, they were in danger of casting into doubt even this belief about him, that he redeems Israel. This did not happen in vain, but to show that “the foolishness of God is wiser than human wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:25). For at the suffering of the cross, all were perplexed and shaken—not only the ordinary disciples, but also the chosen ones and his mother. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sign spoken against and the sword in Mary's soul.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem

comments.capsule: The sword is the Virgin's inexperienced thoughts striking the inward parts, and after the resurrection it no longer bites but gives joy and gladness.
comments.comment: … Simeon called forth the sword of the Virgin's thoughts as striking the inward parts, as approaching scandals, just as the Lord foretold: 'All shall be scandalized in me in this night' (Matthew 26:31). Therefore Simeon also brought forward, saying: 'And from her soul a sword shall pierce' (Luke 2:35), so that thoughts might be revealed from many hearts. Do you see how he called the inexperienced thoughts a sword of thoughts striking the inward parts, approaching the kidneys and marrow? But the Virgin was surrounded by these, not yet knowing the power of the resurrection and that the resurrection does not yet come from neighbors. Therefore after the resurrection, the sword is no longer biting, but joy and gladness. …
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium
comments.work: On the Meeting of the Lord

comments.capsule: The growth of the child is to be received as part of God's plan in the flesh, and the grace of God upon him shows that the Word was and is God even when he appeared as a human.
comments.comment: … So when you hear “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom,” receive the mystery as an account of the economy [God's plan of salvation] with flesh. That he was God in flesh the blessed evangelist himself will confirm, saying that “the grace of God was upon him.” (Luke 2:40) For he is not said to have God’s grace as one who has grace from another god, but because the child had the grace that would befit God. For the Word both was and is God even when he has appeared in flesh, that is, as a human according to us. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Luke's words about the child's growth fit with his being God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Jesus names the one in the heavens as his own Father, and not as the Father of all, because he alone has been begotten from him by nature.
comments.comment: … “And his mother said to him: Child, why have you done thus to us? See, your father and I, being in pain, were seeking you. And he said to them: Why is it that you were seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?” (Luke 2:48–49) Observe how he names as his own Father the one in the heavens. But if he were a human alone, and understood as that very thing according to us, how would it not rather have been necessary to say: Did you not know that I must be in the things of the Father of all? But he makes him his own. For he alone has been begotten from him by nature divinely; and the same one, having also become human, has God as Father by nature and as his own.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Jesus means by 'my Father' at twelve.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature because he emptied himself, and only one who still needs to advance advances.
comments.comment: … And if an example must also be taken from the gospel: Jesus, not yet become a man but still a child, since 'he emptied himself,' was advancing. For no one who is already perfected advances; he advances who still needs advance. So he 'advanced in stature, advanced in wisdom, advanced in grace with God and men.' If he emptied himself coming down here, and emptying himself was taking again from what he had emptied himself of, having emptied himself willingly, what is strange if he also advanced 'in wisdom and stature and grace with God and men,' (Luke 2:52) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jesus could advance in wisdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Isaiah's words about valleys filled and rough places made smooth mean that in Christ even the steep places are smooth for us.
comments.comment: … And this [the way made passable by Christ], I think, is what was spoken through the voice of Isaiah: ‘Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and all the crooked places shall become straight, and the rough places smooth roads’ (Isaiah 40:4; Luke 3:5). For in Christ even the steep places are smooth for us, and rough ground can be walked; the hard roads lie clear and level. Indeed, as the prophet himself says again elsewhere: ‘The way of the godly has become straight, and the way of the godly is made ready’ (Isaiah 26:7). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the levelled road in the quotation means for believers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: John's axe at the root of the trees exposed the uselessness of fruitless wood, and so summoned the people to the fruit-bearing required of them.
comments.comment: … Perhaps John too, being the voice of the Lord, spoke to Israel in a riddle: “Already the axe is laid at the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:9). He was revealing the forests—that is, he was exposing the uselessness of fruits, for a forest is fruitless timber. By showing them its harmful character, he was summoning them to the fruit-bearing that was required of them, saying, “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:8). …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Matthew names Jacob and Luke names Heli as Joseph's father, and the answer starts from one woman, who bore Jacob to Matthan and then Heli to Melchi.
comments.comment: … It is necessary for us to seek by what kind of logic Matthew and Luke disagree (Luke 3:23) concerning Joseph in the genealogy: the one writes Jacob as the son of Matthan, but Luke writes him the son of Heli of Melchi; and how these, being of different generations, both Melchi and Matthan appear as grandfathers of Joseph. This is therefore being made clear. For first Matthan, the one of the lineage of Solomon, takes a wife named Ethan, and from this he begets Jacob, and dies. And Melchi, the one of the lineage of Matthan, takes her, and produces from her Heli. …
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch
comments.work: Commentary on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: Luke ends with 'of God' to set the God who made Adam as the beginning of man, as Christ is head of every man.
comments.comment: [After tracing the line] to Adam, he adds, “of God,” (Luke 3:38) setting the God who made him as the human’s beginning. In the same way we say Christ is every man’s head: for man was made through him and brought into being — the Son not creating him as a mere under-worker, but rather in a God-working way, as Creator by nature. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Luke ends the genealogy with 'of God'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The devil left Christ only until a time, and he came again at the passion.
comments.comment: [On Psalm 22:21, “Save me from the mouth of the lion”:] Here he can also call the devil a "lion", for he attacked in the time of the passion. Indeed, when it was said in the forty-day temptation that "the devil departed from him", it is adjacent in the Gospel to "until a time" (Luke 4:13). Then again, it came when the passion was. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'until an opportune time' points to.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word who fills all things is sent in a human way, to proclaim release, and Scripture uses such human voices to make clear what is beyond our mind.
comments.comment: … Where is the Word of God not present, if he fills all things by the nature of the deity? How then is he sent by the Father? And how does he go to him? So he is sent in a human way, according to the manner and account of the sending, that he may proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind (Luke 4:18) (Isaiah 61:1); yet he goes to the Father and God no longer in the same way, but as embodied, having gone up into heaven, that he may appear for us before the face of the Father (Hebrews 9:24), as it is written. And if “being sent” is also taken of the Word himself, let no one be harsh: for inspired Scripture is sometimes accustomed to use such voices too; and it does not drag the divine and supermundane nature under places and limits — for it knows that nature is bodiless and beyond boundaries and far from being thought of as in a place — but rather tries to make clear, by human voices, the things beyond our mind. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ proclaimed liberty to the captives by releasing those held by the devil and wickedness, forgiving their sins and making them co-heirs with himself.
comments.comment: … For Christ has become to us as wisdom and righteousness and sanctification from God, and also as redemption, saying, 'I was sent to proclaim liberty to the captives' (Luke 4:18). For the redeemer and benefactor of all has released from captivity those held by the devil and by wickedness, forgiving the sins and impieties of those fleeing to him. But his goodness was not satisfied with merely redeeming the captives and their heirs, those of his own father, but he set them as co-heirs of himself, having enjoined upon them an eternal testament, so that possessing it with brevity and perfect readiness, they might receive an immortal inheritance according to the eternal and incorruptible promises. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the release of captives is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words of grace from Christ's mouth hold those who hear them, for all hear the gospel but not all possess the grace of the words.
comments.comment: … Grace was poured out on your lips (Luke 4:22). This is interpreted in the Gospel according to Luke; for how he entered the synagogue in Capernaum, 'and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him' (Luke 4:17), so that it might be read, he said: 'and all were marveling at the words of grace proceeding from his mouth' (Luke 4:22). In this way his words are grace-filled as to hold those who hear. He says 'hearing' according to understanding, not according to mere hearing; for all hear the gospel, and 'Greeks and Jews' (Rom 1:16), but they are not possessing the grace of the words. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'words of grace' the people marveled at.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the days of Elijah and Elisha only one widow and one leper were helped, and Jesus likewise raised only those whom the Word knew to be fit.
comments.comment: … “There were many lepers in the days of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4:27), and “there were many widows in the days of Elijah” the prophet, “and to none of them was Elijah sent except to Zarephath in the land of Sidon” (Luke 4:25–26), for by some divine judgment she had been found worthy of the wonder that the prophet worked with the loaves (1 Kings 17:8–16). In the same way, there were many dead in the days of Jesus, but only those rose whom the Word knew to be fit for resurrection, so that the things done by the Lord might not only be symbols of certain things, but might also, by the deeds themselves, draw many to the wonderful teaching of the gospel. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus cited Zarephath and Naaman, by comparing them with who was raised.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Luke says he rebuked the fever, which suggests that what departs is a living being, and some powers harm the body without blaming the soul of the sufferer.
comments.comment:
The Savior comes to Simon’s house and finds his mother-in-law feverish: ‘and standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left.’

May it not be, then, that in the ‘the fever left her’ as told by Matthew and Mark — where in the whole transaction nothing appears as of a living being effecting the fever — while in the ‘standing over, he rebuked the fever, and it left’ as told by Luke, I do not know, unless we shall be compelled to say that what is rebuked and departs is a living being not admitting the rebuker’s working; for it is not reasonable to say that what is soulless and insensible of rebuke is rebuked.

And it is nothing marvelous that there are certain powers harmful to the human body — and we shall not in every case accuse the soul of the sufferers as being harmed by these; for neither, since the devil, having received authority to tempt him through the body, struck Job with a grievous sore, is Job to be accused on this account — he who contended and nobly endured the blow.

Only let this be said, whenever we are tried by bodily pains: ‘but not his soul’ — as the Lord too, rebuking, heals the sick.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ rebuked the demons even when they cried out the truth, to teach us not to cling to such words, for they weave lies with the truth to harm the hearers.
comments.comment: … Or do you not hear the holy evangelists having written that the demons, crying out something piercing and great, were coming toward Christ: ‘Ah, what to us and to you, Jesus Nazarene? You have come to destroy us; we know who you are, the Holy One of God. Yet he rebuking,’ (Mark 1:24–25) it says, ‘was not allowing them to speak, because they knew him to be the Christ.’ (Luke 4:41) And yet why ever—for according to likelihood someone might hesitate—did Christ rebuke those crying out the true? Yet the thing done was somehow beneficial unto us. For that one must not cling to the words from beside those ones, even if they should wish to cry out the truth itself, and to say the things clearly genuine, we are taught through this; for weaving sometimes the lie with the truth, they harm the hearers, not in another manner, I think, than as one might watch those who by mixture of honey take away the perception of bitter things, and by intertwining of sweet things wish to steal what sometimes grieves. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: In this healing Christ works divinely and bodily together, for the willing is divine and the stretching out of the hand is human.
comments.comment: “I will; be cleansed.” (Luke 5:13) You will marvel in these at Christ working both divinely and bodily together: divine, then, is the willing, but human the stretching out of the hand; so there is one Son from both. For even if the Word became flesh, yet as God he works with his own flesh, which has the power through him (John 1:14). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two sides of the miracle in the leper's healing.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Only God frees from offenses, so Christ's God-befitting authority to forgive shows that he is God, though he is called Son of Man.
comments.comment: … “And Jesus, knowing their thoughts, answered and said to them: Why do you reason in your hearts? Which is easier, to say: Your sins are forgiven you, or to say: Rise and walk? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins — he said to the paralyzed man: I say to you, rise, and taking up your bed go to your house.” (Luke 5:22–24) If only the God of all frees us from offenses, this fitting no one else, and Christ also grants this with God-befitting authority, how would he not be God? For he is called Son of Man, born of a woman according to flesh, though the Word is God. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus' forgiving sins reveals who he is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: God the Word was sent as physician to sinners, calling them to repentance, and as teacher of divine mysteries to those already pure.
comments.comment: Next he [Celsus] misrepresents what has been said and written to exhort those who have lived badly, calling them to repentance (Luke 5:32) and to the reform of their souls, and he says that we claim God was sent to sinners. In this too he acts like someone who would find fault with people for saying that a most humane king had sent the physician because of those in the city who were in a bad way. So God the Word was sent: as physician to sinners (Matthew 9:12), and as teacher of divine mysteries to those who are already pure and no longer sin. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus came for sinners, with the image of a physician.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who weep over a neighbour's sins keep their own gladness, and the laughter promised them is cheerfulness untouched by gloom.
comments.comment: Just as people standing on the shore share the suffering of those drowning in the sea but do not surrender their own safety in their concern for those in danger, so also those who grieve over the sins of their neighbors do not destroy their own gladness. On the contrary, they make it greater, since they are counted worthy of the Lord's joy on account of their tears for a brother. For this reason, blessed are those who weep, and blessed are those who mourn, because they will be comforted, and they will laugh (Matthew 5:4; Luke 6:21). By laughter he does not mean the sound that bursts from the cheeks when the blood boils up, but the cheerfulness that is unmixed and unmingled with anything gloomy. The Apostle therefore permits weeping with those who weep, since this tear becomes, as it were, a seed and a loan of eternal joy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly what the weeping and laughing of the verse mean.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The weeping the Lord blesses differs from the weeping stored up for those who laugh now, and a teacher who moves hearers to tears leads them toward blessed laughter.
comments.comment: And you will seek whether this good laughter, according to one and another sense, agrees with the blessed weeping, but is opposed by another weeping stored up for the opposites. For 'Woe to those who laugh now, for they will mourn and weep' (Luke 6:25)—one weeping is the blessed, another is stored up for those who have lived badly. … Hear Paul. That he taught, he worked at grieving the hearers. And he confesses that then especially he rejoiced when someone was grieved by him; for he says: 'And who is the one who makes me glad if not the one grieved by me?' (2 Corinthians 2:2) And if someone is able to move a hearer’s soul, especially one who has sinned, he prays to speak such words which, announced from power and array and divinity and sacred thoughts, will shake the hearer’s soul and move it unto mourning and unto weeping and unto tears, so that the speaker rejoices when he sees the hearing turned and filled upon what is said. For where he leads unto promises, as through the narrow and afflicted way in being grieved unto life, he also leads through weeping unto the blessed laughter.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Giving cheerfully is good, but better is the Lord's command to give to everyone who asks, since such generosity is God's own.
comments.comment: The apostle's word is good: "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7)—one who rejoices in giving and does not sow sparingly, so that he may not reap in the same way; one who shares without grumbling, division, or grief, which is pure beneficence. But better than this is what the Lord said in another place: "Give to everyone who asks you" (Luke 6:30). For such generosity is truly God's own.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how far the command to give to everyone goes.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: God's kindness to the ungrateful and evil shows his compassion, and he bears with those who stray to give them time for repentance.
comments.comment: God’s feeding even sinners and being kind to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35) testifies to his compassion, not his malice. He does not wish the death of one who dies, but that the person turn back and live (Ezekiel 18:32). He does not quickly punish those who stray. He does this for no other purpose than that his goodness may grant time for repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Says why God is kind to the ungrateful and evil, in terms any reader can follow.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: God's mercy shows most when the one who receives is ungrateful, and he is kind even to such people.
comments.comment: And I say: then the mercy and the benevolence appear, if the receiver is ungrateful. 'He is kind even to the ungrateful and the evil,' Luke 6:35 he gives. Those receiving are ungrateful—for by not giving back what is necessary to give back, they are found ungrateful and evil—but God is still kind even to these. Therefore the righteous even more shows mercy and provides.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Do not judge who deserves help, for giving to everyone in need will reach some who are loved by God.
comments.comment:
Do not judge who is worthy and who is unworthy, for you may miss the mark in your judgment. Since the matter is uncertain through ignorance, it is better to do good even to the unworthy for the sake of the worthy than to be on guard and, by avoiding the less good, fail to encounter the excellent. For from sparing and pretending to test who will rightly receive or not, you may neglect some who are loved by God, and the penalty for that is fiery eternal punishment. But from giving to all in turn who are in need, you must certainly find some who are able to be saved with God.

"Do not judge, then, so that you may not be judged; with the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you; a good measure, pressed down and shaken and running over, will be given to you" (Luke 6:38; cf. Matthew 7:1-2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the command not to judge by applying it to giving.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Those who give freely imitate God's kindness, and the heavenly king receives the willing so that by giving they receive.
comments.comment: For the rest he commands continual sharing and giving from what they have, so that through these things they may be found imitators of God’s kindness, showing mercy, sharing, and giving freely. “Give,” he says, “and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:38). … For the heavenly king does not compel, nor does he demand tribute, but he receives those who are eager, so that by giving they may receive, by honoring they may be honored, and by sharing in temporary things they may be called to share in eternal things.
comments.selected_reason: Shows what the promise of being given in return means.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: To call Jesus Lord truly is to serve him in deeds, thoughts and words, doing the will of the Father, and not merely to say the word.
comments.comment: He who serves God calls him 'Lord' through his deeds, his mindsets, and his words. This one says, 'In the Holy Spirit, Lord Jesus'; for not everyone who calls Jesus Lord does so in this Spirit, but hypocrites indeed do this. Many will say to me on that day, 'Lord, Lord' (Matthew 7:21-23), and what does he say to them? 'I never knew you.' I never knew you having served me. And again: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say?' (Luke 6:46). Therefore, he who calls Jesus thus Lord, doing the will of his Father in heaven, is the one who calls him 'in the Holy Spirit' Lord. The voice is therefore that of a slave.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to call Jesus Lord and not do what he says.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Seeing the widow's son raised made the resurrection of Adam certain, since the earth was like a widow when her first-formed son died.
comments.comment: So they learned, and were made certain of, the resurrection of Adam when they saw the Lord raise the widow’s son (Luke 7:12–15); for the earth became like a widow when her son, the first-formed man, died. And when they saw Him raise the daughter of the synagogue ruler (Luke 8:49–55), they were made wise to know that He will raise Eve too, together with Adam.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: That Christ dines with a Pharisee shows his love for humanity, since he also does not shun tax collectors and sinners.
comments.comment: In order that you may know also the philanthropy of Christ, and the irrationality of the Pharisees, and the turning back of the sinner, I will set before you those evangelical sayings; for if you listen to the style of the reading, you will easily grasp the sense of the interpretation. One of the Pharisees, he says, asked Jesus to eat with him. And having entered into the house of the Pharisee, he reclined (Luke 7:36). O unutterable grace! O unspeakable philanthropy! And he dines with Pharisees, and does not shun tax collectors, and receives fornicatresses, and converses with a Samaritan woman (John 4:7), and deems a Canaanite woman worthy of a word (Matthew 15:22), and grants the basin to the woman with the hemorrhage (Mark 5:25).
comments.selected_reason: Shows what Jesus' acceptance of the invitation reveals about him.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Christ went to the Pharisee's table to show his body was real and to teach the Pharisees how God honors sinners who turn from their sins.
comments.comment: First, in order to sanctify those called, the one who called the woman arranged the arrangement of the house and the abundance of food; then showing that the incarnation was not a phantom, from the reclining, the eating, the drinking, and the expenditure on provisions. Furthermore, because the harlot was about to approach and show that fervent and fiery way of repentance, for this reason, in calling the Pharisee, he sympathizes quickly, so that, having theatrically exposed the domestic evils before the eyes of scribes and Pharisees, he might teach them how sinners, loathing at sins, must be honored by God. Behold, he says, a woman in the city, who was a sinner (Luke 7:37). Woman: the easily deceived nature, the first net of the devil, the introduction to error, the teacher of transgression, having become a helper indeed but having been revealed as a war, having been born good according to nature but having been shown evil by choice, the bringer of death, she who showed the beauty of the tree and lost the whole paradise. And behold, a woman, he says, in the city, who was a sinner, bearing the burdens of Eve, being covered by many evils. And I shall speak of the abundance of her former evils, so that you may know the abundance of her repentance.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The women whom Jesus had healed supplied the disciples with food from their own means, which is no disgrace, since philosophers also received what they needed from their pupils.
comments.comment: He also says that Jesus “went about with his disciples collecting their food in a disgraceful and beggarly way.” Let him tell us where he found the disgrace and the beggarliness in this collecting. For in the Gospels “certain women” who “had been healed of” their “infirmities,” among whom was “Susanna,” provided the disciples with food “out of their own means” (Luke 8:2–3). Which of those who practised philosophy and devoted themselves to the good of their pupils did not receive from them what they needed? Or did the philosophers do this fittingly and well, while the disciples of Jesus, when they do the same, are accused by Celsus of “collecting their food in a disgraceful and beggarly way”?
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how the healed women supported Jesus and the disciples.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What is taken from the one who has not is the remnant of virtue and knowledge of God, lost by those who used them badly.
comments.comment: Take away his garment, for an insolent man passes by who plunders what belongs to others. This is that which is said in the Gospel: 'And from him who has not, even what he seems to have will be taken away' (Luke 8:18). This shows, in my opinion, the intellectual remnants of virtues and the knowledge of God being taken from men who have used them badly.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Christ rebuking the wind and sea shows him to be truly God, for Scripture says of God that he rules the might of the sea and calms its waves.
comments.comment: The disciples, he says, were being storm-tossed on the lake; then “coming they woke him saying: Master, we are perishing. And having been woken he rebuked the wind and the surge of the water, and it ceased and there was a calm.” (Luke 8:24) It has been said about Christ through the voice of the blessed David: “You rule the might of the sea; you calm the tossing of its waves; the heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the inhabited world and its fullness.” (Psalm 89:9–12) So what would fit the one who calms the sea if not also to rule all things? And to have the heavens as his own, and to be able to found the inhabited world and its fullness — how would Christ not be understood to be truly God, the one who rebukes sea and winds, and that with authority?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the calming of the storm shows who Christ is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ sent the healed man to proclaim what God had done because he worked as God, crushing Satan by his own power and not as a servant of grace like a prophet.
comments.comment: In the country of the Gerasenes Christ healed the man fiercely demonized, who also begged to be with him. But though he had healed him and cast out the spirits, he ordered him to go to his house and proclaim how much God had done for him. So he himself worked as being true God. For we do not say somewhere that he became a minister of divine grace, like one of the prophets or of the holy apostles; rather he himself was crushing Satan by his own and God-befitting power. So in his name the demons were also subjected to the holy disciples, and they themselves confessed this.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ sent the man to tell of what God had done.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Only the woman touched Jesus by faith, with the inner man's touch, and so power went out to heal her, while the crowds pressing him did not touch him.
comments.comment: The outer man has perceptible touch, and the inner man has touch — that touch by which the woman with the flow of blood touched the hem of Jesus. She touched. For the one who said, Who touched me? bore witness. And a little before, Peter was saying to him: The crowds are pressing you, and you say, Who touched me? He thinks that those who touch bodily are touching, not spiritually. So those pressing Jesus were not touching him; for they were not touching him by faith. But she alone, having a certain divine touch, touched Jesus and for this reason was healed. And since she touched with his divine touch, for this reason power of Jesus went out upon her divine touch
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why her touch differed from the crowd's pressing.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ spoke truly in saying the girl did not die, because to God, who is God of the living, those who are to live are not dead.
comments.comment: About the synagogue ruler’s daughter Christ says: “Do not weep; for the girl did not die, but is sleeping.” (Luke 8:52) So was he lying? Far from it — he speaks truth. And in what way? Because it is written: “He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” (Luke 20:38) For they live to God who are going to live; therefore the dead are dead according to humans, but according to the life-giving nature — that is, the divine — they have not died. So he speaks truth as God when he says about the girl: “She did not die, but is sleeping.”
comments.selected_reason: Answers the question how Christ could say the girl was not dead.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Jesus did not appear the same to all, which is why only Peter, James and John, who could take in his glory, went up the mountain and saw Moses and Elijah.
comments.comment: Jesus, though one, was many in aspect; and he was not seen alike by all who saw him. … That even when seen he did not appear the same to all who saw him, but according to what each beholder could receive, will be clear to those who consider why, when he was about to be transfigured on the high mountain, he did not take even all the apostles, but only Peter and James and John (Matthew 17:1–2). For they alone could take in the sight of his glory at that time, and were able also to perceive Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory (Luke 9:30–31), and to hear them talking together, and the voice from heaven out of the cloud (Matthew 17:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ led us up the high mountain of the Word and showed his glory together with the spiritual law, Moses, and the whole of prophecy, symbolized by Elijah.
comments.comment: And having dwelt and come to be among us, he did not stay in his first form. He led us up onto the “high mountain” (Matthew 17:1) of the Word and showed us his glorious form and the brightness of his garments (Matthew 17:2), and not his own only, but also that of the spiritual law, which is “Moses,” seen “in glory” with Jesus (Luke 9:30–31). He showed us also the whole of prophecy, which did not die even after he became man, but was taken up into heaven; Elijah was its symbol (2 Kings 2:11). And one who has gazed on these things could say: “We beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).
comments.selected_reason: Says what Moses and Elijah stand for in the scene.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The voice from the cloud was heard only by those who went up with Jesus, since God's voice is heard by a higher hearing than that of the senses.
comments.comment: Moreover, the voice from the cloud on the very high mountain was heard only by those who had gone up with him (Matthew 17:1–5; compare Mark 9:2–7; Luke 9:28–35). For the divine voice is of such a kind that it is heard only by those whom the speaker wishes to hear it. I do not yet add that the voice of God recorded in Scripture is by no means struck air, or a stroke of air, or whatever else it is called in the treatises on voice, and that for this reason it is heard by a hearing higher and more divine than the hearing of the senses. And whenever the speaker wishes his voice not to be audible to all, the one who “has” the higher “ears” (Matthew 13:9) hears God, while the one whose soul’s hearing has been deafened does not perceive God speaking.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why only some heard the voice.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A plowman who turns to look behind him breaks the furrow and spoils the work, so this turning back is blamed, while turning back in repentance is praised.
comments.comment: The word 'backwards' is used differently in various places of the Scripture. The phrase 'to turn back to the rear' carries a reproach. For instance, the wife of Lot, leaving from that place of destruction, heard: 'do not look to the rear' (Genesis 19:17), meaning, do not set your heart upon that which you are leaving behind. Again, in other places it is said: 'my enemies turned back to the rear.' They turned back to their own rear, so that they might no longer pursue the same path as enemies. 'No one, having laid his hand to the plow, and having turned to the rear' (Luke 9:62). It was not said 'of someone,' but simply 'to the rear'; for when the plowman turns, he breaks the furrow. And the breaking of the furrow hinders the work. It is said that someone turns himself to the rear; this is praised, but this is a reproach. If one hastens to flee a path and turns, this turning to the rear is a reproach. But if someone is pressed toward evil and is checked and turns back by words of repentance, this turning which comes from repentance is praised.
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes the blamed turning back from the praised one.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Preachers must go straight to the work, since stopping for others costs zeal and preaching time.
comments.comment: …“Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals; and greet no one on the road” (Luke 10:4). For one must go to the work with a straight course, and not even return a blessing to one who blesses. For turning aside to others is a loss to zeal, and so is spending idly, on things that are not necessary, the time that belongs to preaching; nor should one grant friendships the favor of useless delay. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ forbids even greetings on the road.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ names lightning to show how swift the devil's fall was, not the place he fell from.
comments.comment: …Even if the Lord says, "I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven" (Luke 10:18), he is not indicating the place from which he fell. Rather, since lightning falls swiftly from above, he compared the swiftness of the devil's fall to lightning, saying: as lightning rushes swiftly from heaven, so I saw his fall as swift. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of lightning in plain terms.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The healed receive authority to tread on the serpents and scorpions of wickedness and are not harmed.
comments.comment: …And these lame who have been healed receive from Jesus “authority to tread,” with the very feet in which they were formerly lame, “upon” the “serpents and scorpions” of wickedness, and in a word “over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19); and as they tread they are not harmed, for they too have become stronger than the venom of all wickedness and of the demons.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through faith we have authority over snakes and scorpions, so the faithless should fear their own faithlessness more than wild beasts.
comments.comment: The wild beasts are a demonstration of faith. Have you trusted in the Lord? Upon asp and basilisk you will tread, and you will trample lion and dragon (Psalm 90:13 (LXX; Hebrew 91:13)). And you have through faith the authority to tread upon snakes and scorpions (Luke 10:19). Or do you not see that when Paul was gathering sticks, the viper fastened on him and caused him no harm, because the holy man was found to be full of faith (Acts 28:3-5)? But if you are faithless, fear not so much the wild beast as your own faithlessness, through which you have made yourself easy prey to every corruption. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: The names written in the heavens are the qualities that mark the disciples, not letters combined on a page.
comments.comment: …But of the disciples, 'the names are written in the heavens' (Luke 10:20). He does not speak of these designations by combining letters, but of the very qualities which signify them, for the definition of a name is given thus: a name is a principal designation representing the quality of the one named. This is the descriptive name: man, heaven. 'Is written,' therefore, that is, has been arranged. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for names to be written in heaven.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Names are inscribed in the heavens according to virtue, not by gathering letters together.
comments.comment: …The Savior says, therefore: 'Do not rejoice that the demons are subject to you, but that your names are inscribed in the heavens' (Luke 10:20). And it is not necessary anywhere to reason thus, that names are inscribed in the heavens by gathering them together, but names according to virtue; these things have the heavens in eternal memory. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Savior is the neighbor who showed mercy, healing our wounds with the wine and oil he poured out.
comments.comment: [The Samaritan who cared for the wounded man:] …Who else could this be but the Savior himself? Or who has shown us more mercy than he—us, who were nearly put to death by the world-rulers of the darkness with many wounds: fears, desires, fits of anger, griefs, deceptions, pleasures? Of these wounds the only physician is Jesus, who cuts out the passions completely, root and branch. He does not do what the law does, which deals only with the bare results, the fruits of the wicked plants; instead he brings his own axe to the roots of evil. This is the one who poured out the wine—the blood of the vine of David—upon our wounded souls. This is the one who brought the oil—the mercy from the Father's bowels—and lavished it on us. This is the one who showed us the unbreakable bonds of health and salvation: love, faith, hope. This is the one who commanded angels and rulers and authorities to serve us for a great reward, because they too will be set free from the futility of the world at the revelation of the glory of the sons of God. …
comments.selected_reason: Reads the Samaritan's care of the wounded man in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Christ rebukes the soul that frets over many things like Martha, since the one thing needed is to hear the Word.
comments.comment: …You have the Lord Jesus rebuking the soul striving for such things like Martha (Luke 10:41-42), and saying: 'Why are you anxious about many things and troubled? One thing is necessary,' to hear the divine Word, and after this, to be sharp in all that is found. Therefore he also immediately brings forth saying: 'Mary has chosen the good portion, which shall not be taken away from her' (Luke 10:42). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Christ means by the one thing needed.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Debts are the duties we owe in giving, speech and works, which we pay by doing the law or leave unpaid, and Luke's 'sins' means the same, since sins are unpaid debts.
comments.comment:
'And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matthew 6:12) — or as Luke has it, 'And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (Luke 11:4) Concerning debts, the Apostle says: 'Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute, fear to whom fear, tax to whom tax, honor to whom honor. Owe no one anything, except to love one another.' (Romans 13:7) We owe, then — holding certain duties — not only in giving, but in gentle speech too, and in certain works; and we owe a certain disposition toward them. These debts we either pay, by performing what the divine law commands, or, by despising the wholesome word, not paying, we remain in owing. …

But Luke, saying 'Forgive us our sins' — since sins are debts of debtors who owe and pay not — says the same as Matthew …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'debts' means in the prayer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
