comments.capsule: Luke's 'bring us not into temptation' also teaches 'deliver us from evil,' for God delivers us when we conquer what befalls us.
comments.comment: Luke, I take it, through the 'bring us not into temptation,' (Luke 11:4) taught in effect the 'deliver us from evil' (Matthew 6:13) too. …And God 'delivers us' 'from evil' — not when the enemy in no way approaches us, wrestling, with whatever methods of his, and serving his own will — but when we conquer, standing manfully toward what befalls. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not all asking receives, only asking according to the will of God.
comments.comment: …'the one asking receives' (Luke 11:10) does not mean that all people, asking haphazardly, receive the same things that do not benefit them, but rather those containing the request according to the will of God. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the limit on the promise that the one asking receives.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Luke's 'Holy Spirit' stands for the good gifts, since the Spirit is good by nature.
comments.comment: He calls “good gifts” (Matthew 7:11) the spiritual gifts. Luke said “Holy Spirit” (Luke 11:13) instead of “goods,” and there is no difference: the Holy Spirit is what is good by nature. That is why he also gives goods to those who share in him. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Luke says 'Holy Spirit' where Matthew says good gifts.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Luke's 'Holy Spirit' is Matthew's 'good things,' for the one Spirit is many good things in his gifts.
comments.comment: …And the other Evangelist, the Holy Spirit, interpreted the good things; for writing in the same place, Matthew says: 'He will give good things to those asking Him' (Matthew 7:11), while Luke says: 'He will give the Holy Spirit' (Luke 11:13). The Spirit, being one, is a multitude of good things according to His various gifts; for he who has the Holy Spirit has the gifts of the Spirit, which are many good things. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ says a lamp is set on a lampstand to show that those who serve as priests in the gospel will be conspicuous.
comments.comment: …That is why Christ too said that those who serve as priests in proclaiming the gospel to the nations (Romans 15:16), and to those of Israel besides, would be conspicuous in every way and without fail, and would receive a glory on which all eyes are fixed. ‘For no one, after lighting a lamp, puts it in a hidden place, nor even under a bed,’ he says, ‘or under a basket, but on the lampstand, so that all who come in may see the light.’ (Luke 11:33; Luke 8:16) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 13

comments.capsule: Those who kill the body can do nothing after it, since a slain body has no sensation.
comments.comment: …The Truth would never have said, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28), if anything that enemies might choose to do with the bodies of the slain could harm the life to come. Unless someone is so absurd as to argue that those who kill the body should not be feared before death, lest they kill the body, but should be feared after death, lest they not allow the slain body to be buried. Is it false, then, what the Truth says: "those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do" (Luke 12:4), if they have so much they can do with the corpses? Far be it that what the Truth said should be false. For it says they do something when they kill, because there is sensation in the body while it is being killed; but after that they have nothing they can do, because there is no sensation in a slain body. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'have nothing more they can do' in plain terms.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: The rich man called earthly abundance goods, but the truly good things are in heaven.
comments.comment: …He has judged the grain and the abundance of earthly things to be goods; for he did not see that the truly good things are not in the cursed earth, but the truly good things are in heaven. He was treasuring on earth, because he thought the things on earth were goods. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is wrong with the man's words to his soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever carries wealth in his heart is bound to the earth, for where a person's mind is, there is his treasure.
comments.comment: …But the one who carries wealth in his soul, and instead of the Spirit of God carries gold or a field in his heart, and always makes his possession boundless and is always looking for more, bent downward and bound by the snares of the world, being earth and about to go away into earth—how can such a one desire or care about the kingdom of heaven? A human being wearing not a heart but a field or a mine, who will necessarily be found in the things he has chosen? For where a person's mind is, there also is his treasure (Luke 12:34). …
comments.selected_reason: Shows plainly what the saying about treasure and heart means.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: We must be ready every day to depart, watching for the Master's signal.
comments.comment: …We do not consider that we must be ready every day for our departure from here, waiting with fixed eyes for the Master's signal. For He says, "Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like people waiting for their master to return from the wedding feast, so that when he comes and knocks, they may open to him at once" (Luke 12:35-36). …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things

comments.capsule: Being girded and lit means not being entangled when the day comes and keeping faith awake for the Lord's knock.
comments.comment: …We must be girded, so that when the day of departure comes, it does not find us hindered and entangled. Let our light shine and blaze in good works, so that it may lead us from this night of the world to the light of eternal glory. Let us wait, always anxious and careful, for the sudden coming of the Lord, so that when he knocks, our faith may wake up and receive from the Lord the reward of watchfulness. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the girded loins, burning lamps and waiting for the knock in plain words.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Even sin in ignorance is liable to judgment, but the punishment is heavier for those who know.
comments.comment: …It is agreed that even sinning in ignorance is liable to judgment. But that the punishment will be heavier for those who know, the Savior has made fully certain when he says, “The one who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know and does not do it will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48). It is agreed, then, that it is better to sin in ignorance than with knowledge of the laws. …
comments.selected_reason: States the point of the many and few blows plainly.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The greater the dignity given, the greater the service demanded.
comments.comment: …To whom much is given, much is required from him (Luke 12:48), and to whom more of dignity is ascribed, more of service is demanded from him. …
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: Christ came longing for our salvation, casting fire on the earth to rekindle the freedom it had from the beginning, which the deceiver had enslaved to passions.
comments.comment: Longing for our salvation, he cried out elsewhere, saying, 'I came to cast fire upon the earth' (Luke 12:49), the one who desires mercy, the one who thirsts to thirst, the one who swore by himself, 'not to desire the death of the sinner, but that he might turn back and live.' The Savior came to cast fire upon the earth, which he fashioned with his own hands and sanctified with the divine breath. The Savior came to cast fire upon it to rekindle its self-power [freedom of choice], which was honored by him from the beginning, but which the finder of evil and deceit took away from it and enslaved in passions of dishonor. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ came to cast fire.
comments.author: Eustathius of Antioch

comments.capsule: The fire Christ came to cast burns up former sins and turns a person toward repentance.
comments.comment: …For if anyone receives in his mind the salvation-fire, about which the Savior said, 'I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want, if it is already kindled' (Luke 12:49), he burns up the former sins; and sitting, instead of 'having ceased from sinning,' he is turned toward repentance, choosing a somewhat severe and rigorous life. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many are bent double under Satan, who wants us to look downward, and only the Word sets them upright.
comments.comment: …It is written in the Gospel that a certain woman “was bent double and unable to straighten herself fully” (Luke 13:11). When Jesus saw her, and saw why she was bent double, not being allowed to straighten herself “fully”, he said, “And this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound for eighteen long years, ought she not to have been loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13:16). How many others now, bound by Satan, are bent double, unable because of him to “straighten themselves fully”, since he wants us to look downward? And no one sets them upright except the Word who came to dwell in Jesus, and who also inspired men before that. Jesus came to set free “all who were oppressed by the devil” (Acts 10:38). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's saying charges the people with violence against every holy man, as their treatment of John had just shown.
comments.comment: …Yet the Jews took delight in John for a very short time, in that they ran to the baptism he gave and marveled greatly at him; then they put the ever-shining lamp to sleep in death, all but quenching it. For even if the crime may perhaps be called Herod’s (Matthew 14:10), still he was of Israel’s blood. That is why Christ, charging the peoples of the Jews with their insolence against every holy man, says: ‘It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem’ (Luke 13:33). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says a prophet perishes in Jerusalem.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: Those called from the nations do not refuse the call as the first invited did, but answer it at once.
comments.comment: … In the Gospel parables some of those first invited said, 'I have married a wife; excuse me,' and another, 'I have bought five yoke of oxen and am going to test them (Luke 14:19); excuse me.' We from the nations are not called and then refuse like that. Over what field would we settle? Over what wise wife? Over what else would we busy ourselves? God has said to us, 'Return, you turning children, and I will heal your broken places.' Seeing our broken places and the promise of healing, we answer at once …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The saying about hating family cannot mean real hatred, since the Lord also commands love of enemies; it means breaking from anyone who hinders faith.
comments.comment: … But let this not disturb us, nor the still harsher saying uttered elsewhere in the words: “Whoever does not hate father and mother and children, and even his own soul, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). For the God of peace is not introducing hatred and separation from those most loved—he who urges us to love even our enemies. If enemies must be loved, then by the same reasoning, moving upward from them, so must those nearest in family; or if those of one's own blood must be hated, then the saying, moving downward, teaches that enemies must be hated far more, so that the two sayings would be shown to refute each other. But they do not refute each other, nor come close. For from the same mind and disposition and on the same principle a person would hate a father and love an enemy—one who neither takes revenge on an enemy nor reverences a father more than Christ. In the one saying he cuts out hatred and wrongdoing; in the other, the deference toward intimates. If it harms salvation—if, say, a father or son or brother is godless to someone and becomes a hindrance to faith and an obstacle to the life above—let him not join with that one or be of one mind with him, but let him dissolve the fleshly kinship because of the spiritual enmity.
comments.selected_reason: Resolves the hard saying about hating father and mother in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Hating father and mother means not preferring them to God, especially in a time of persecution.
comments.comment: To prefer something over God. Since God is to be loved most in a time of struggle, in a time of persecution, the love of God must be preferred above all. If one pulls away from parents or the old age of a parent, 'honor God, since you are not able to follow me' (Exodus 20:12). Therefore, to hate the father and the mother does not mean that kind of hatred by which we are provoked and loathe, but rather according to not preferring them to God. In this same way, one treats the wife and the children, and in this same way, the brothers. 'And he will hate even his own soul' (Luke 14:26), he says. He hates his own soul while enduring death for the sake of a witness, but on account of the Savior; for see what he says: he who hates a father 'because of me' (Matthew 10:37), not completely. The Savior is to be preferred above all. Just as if someone hates a mother because of the Savior. This hatred does not bring slander. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine safe in the fold to seek the one, lest it be lost and fall to the devil.
comments.comment: … For he is the one seeking the lost sheep, having left the ninety-nine and going about the search for the one. For he seeks the one, neither regarding the many nor preferring the one over the multitude. But since he left the ninety-nine, for it was necessary that they be safely penned in the fold, he went circling to seek the one, so that he might not be lost and become the devil's. For a lost sheep is a ready supper for beasts and an unsealed soul, vulnerable to demons. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek one sheep.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Patience searches for the wandering sheep and carries it back, where impatience would despise it.
comments.comment: … The shepherd's patience seeks and finds the wandering sheep (Luke 15:4-6). Impatience would easily despise a single sheep, but patience undertakes the labor of the search, and carries the abandoned sinner back on his shoulders, a patient bearer. …
comments.selected_reason: Shows what the shepherd's search and carrying home mean.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: The doors are open to everyone who turns to God with a true heart, and heaven rejoices over each sinner who repents.
comments.comment: … the doors have been opened to everyone who turns to God with truth from the whole heart, and the Father receives with exceeding joy a son who truly repents. True repentance is no longer being liable to the same sins, but rooting out completely from the soul the sins for which one has condemned oneself to death. For when these are destroyed, God will again take up residence in you. For he says that there is great and unsurpassable joy and a feast in heaven for the Father and the angels when one sinner turns and repents (Luke 15:7, 10). …
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: A soul that has lost its treasure through laziness should light the lamp of repentance and seek it.
comments.comment: … You had the evangelical drachma and were enriching yourself well with the money, then through laziness you lost it. Light the lamp of repentance (Luke 15:8), bow down with care, seek the treasure hidden to the poor through afflictions (Matt 13:44). Having found it, lift it up and save it, …
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: The son who left his father by his own choice paid for his wasteful table with the food of swine.
comments.comment: … There is a story of a son who received from his father the share of the inheritance that fell to him, as against his other brother, and went abroad from his father into a far country, by his own choice. Living wastefully, he scattered his father's property and used it up. At last, in his want, he hired himself out to feed swine. Driven by hunger, he longed even to share the swine's food, yet he could not get even this (Luke 15:12–16). So he paid the penalty for his wasteful table: in exchange for his father's table, which was a royal one, he received what he had not foreseen, the food of swine and the food of a hired laborer. …
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The son who left his father's house was a stranger to himself, and in repenting he came back into himself.
comments.comment: … he who departed from his father's house became a stranger outside of himself; his soul was no longer his own. But indeed, when he repented, he says: 'having entered into himself' (Luke 15:17). Consequently, he became his own; his soul consequently became his own. This is similar to 'know thyself.' He who knows himself is within himself. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the son 'came to himself'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good steward is ready to leave his stewardship as Paul was, while the earthly man laments helplessly like the steward in the parable.
comments.comment: … Are we being moved from our stewardship? But the good and faithful steward, having trusted in his own management, has a will such as Paul had. For he, when the Lord was not hurrying, hastened to him and desired the dismissal and was willing to relinquish the stewardship, saying in one way: 'Wretched am I a man, who will rescue me from this body of death?' (Rom 7:24) and again: 'For to me it is good to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23). But the earthly man, whose mindset is truly kin to the oxen, laments such things helplessly at the transition, like this man in the parable: 'What shall I do, since my lord is taking the stewardship from me? I am not able to dig, and I am ashamed to beg' (Luke 16:3). …
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: The sons of this age are called more prudent only in their own generation, in the things of this age, and not wiser absolutely.
comments.comment: … Again the same Savior says: 'The sons of this age are more prudent than the sons of light, in their own generation' (Luke 16:8); calling sons of light those who have been enlightened by the knowledge of the truth and by the works of virtue. Toward whom he says, 'You are the light of the world' (Matt 5:14), because they are children of light; but those loving the present life, and lifting up all things toward it which they do, he named sons of this age. But even if he said these are more prudent than the sons of light, he did not say they are more prudent absolutely, but in their own generation; that is, in the things pertaining to this age, they are found more prudent than the sons of light. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording of the Lord's remark about the sons of this age and the sons of light.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Feeding the hungry and sheltering the homeless need money, so a command to give it all up would set the Lord's teaching against itself.
comments.comment: And how much more useful is the opposite [of casting away one's possessions]: to have enough, so that you neither suffer hardship over your possessions yourself nor fail to help those you ought to help? For what sharing would be left among human beings if no one had anything? How could this teaching not be found plainly opposed to many other fine teachings of the Lord, and fighting against them? "Make friends for yourselves by means of worldly wealth, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings" (Luke 16:9). "Store up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal" (Matthew 6:20). How could anyone feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, or take in the homeless—things for which he threatens fire and outer darkness to those who do not do them—if each person were already lacking all these things himself? … But if it is not possible to fulfill these needs without money, and he commands us to give up money, what else would the Lord be doing but urging the same things to be given and not given, to feed and not to feed, to take in and to shut out, to share and not to share—which is the most irrational thing of all.
comments.selected_reason: Shows from the verse itself that wealth is meant to be used for others.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Lazarus is described as utterly destitute, sick and thrown at the rich man's gate, to expose the hardness of the one who showed no mercy.
comments.comment: … There was once a man named Lazarus (Luke 16:20). The word does not describe him as a mere poor man, but as one deprived of the necessities of spending and need, and also being tormented by painful sickness and having a body broken, homeless, unsupported, untreated, thrown at the gate of the rich. And with great care in the narration, he brings the misfortunes of the poor to a tragic climax, so as to expose the hardness of the one who does not show mercy. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the parable describes Lazarus' misery in such detail.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: Angels served the poor man at his death, carrying him and looking on him calmly and gently.
comments.comment: … And it happened that the poor man died and was carried by the angels into the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22). Do you see the ministers of the righteous and the poor, and the servants of the transfer? For angels were bearing him, looking at him calmly and gently, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the angels' carrying of Lazarus.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: The poor man had angels as guards, while the rich man is said only to have been buried, and that one word shows his dishonorable end.
comments.comment: … It is also worthy to test the departure of another of the dead. For the poor man, having fallen asleep, had angels as guards and attendants, leading him with good hope to the place of rest; but the rich man, having died, is said to have been buried (Luke 16:22). For there is nothing like using that scriptural word, which through a single word sufficiently interprets the dishonorable dissolution of the rich. …
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: The angels who carried the poor man show that angels are present both here and among the dead and carry there whomever God wills.
comments.comment: … For if there were no angels who could be present in the places of both the living and the dead, the Lord Jesus would not have said: “It happened that the poor man died and was carried away by the angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22). Therefore they were able to be now here, now there, who carried from here to there whomever God willed—namely, the angels. …
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: The rich man, stripped of what he thought he ruled, begs from afar for the mercy he did not give when it was easy.
comments.comment: … when he is snatched away from life and, like a slave of lashes, is deprived of those things of which through ignorance he thought himself a master, humility is imposed upon him in response to his pride. Like a goat putting forward the wails of a mourning woman, he calls upon the patriarch from afar and ignorantly, saying: 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am suffering in this flame' (Luke 16:24), seeking a mercy which was not given when it was easy for him to do good because he possessed the authority; and demanding that Lazarus arrive to help against the fire, praying to suck the finger of the leper slightly moistened with water. Such are the follies of the flesh-lovers; this is the end of the lovers of wealth and the lovers of pleasure. …
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: Those who spend wealth on the flesh now and promise to obey later will hear Abraham say they received their good things in life.
comments.comment: Why then do you deceive yourself, spending your wealth badly now on the enjoyment of flesh, while promising for later what you will no longer be master of? As the word has shown, the plan is wicked: While I live, I will enjoy pleasures; when I die, I will do what has been commanded. Abraham will also say to you: "You received your good things in your life" (Luke 16:25). The narrow and afflicted way does not receive you, since you have not put off the bulk of wealth. You went out carrying it; for you did not throw it away, as you were commanded. While you lived, you put yourself before the commandment; after death and dissolution, then you preferred the commandment of your enemies. "So that so-and-so does not get it," he says, "let the Lord take it. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The great chasm is a picture of the separation of those who lived by virtue from those who lived otherwise, not a ditch actually dug.
comments.comment: … Moreover, he says there is a great chasm, which prevents them from intermingling with one another, and it separates those punishing from those being punished, so that both may clearly distinguish themselves from one another, having an unmixed enjoyment of the good and the evil. I think the sensory parable is an enigma of an intellectual theory. For let us not truly suppose a ditch actually dug there among the angels, like the trenches that happen in military camps, but Luke describes to us the separation of those who are divided from one another, both those according to virtue and those who lived otherwise, setting forth the image of the chasm (Luke 16:26). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the great chasm means.
comments.author: Asterius of Amasea

comments.capsule: Faith is not only believing that God is one but standing firm in soul and being ready to walk with the Lord, which the disciples asked to have increased.
comments.comment: … Faith here would be, as I think, steadfastness toward every good thing whatever, and toward whatever God may will. For in this sense we say that Moses, the revealer of holy things, was faithful “in all his house” (Hebrews 3:2; Numbers 12:7). For faith would not be understood or spoken of as only the duty to believe that by nature and in truth there is one God of all, but as standing firm in soul, “and being ready to walk with the Lord God,” in the words of the prophet (Micah 6:8). And so the inspired disciples once came to Christ, saying plainly, “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what faith means in the disciples' request.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Doing only what is commanded makes an unprofitable servant, while going beyond it is doing what one ought.
comments.comment: … Hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in it and saying: when you have done all that is commanded you, you ought to say we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10). And if, when I do all that is commanded, I am an unprofitable servant, when will I flee being an unprofitable servant? If being more ambitious you ascend from what is commanded; for example: if I keep "you shall not commit adultery" and not looking at a woman to desire her, I have done what I ought. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom is within us, so whoever prays for it prays that it bear fruit in himself.
comments.comment: 'Thy kingdom come.' The 'kingdom of God,' according to the word of our Lord and Savior, 'comes not with observation,' 'nor shall they say: Lo here, or lo there' (Luke 17:20–21) — but 'the kingdom of God is within' us ('for the word is very nigh, in our mouth and in our heart' (Deuteronomy 30:14)). So it is plain that the one who prays for God's kingdom to come rightly prays concerning God's kingdom in himself — that it rise and bear fruit and be perfected. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains where the kingdom of God is and what it means to pray for it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom is a disposition, not a place.
comments.comment: … The kingdom of the heavens is not in a place but in a disposition, for it is within us (Luke 17:21). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The good is within us by natural inclination to virtue, while sin's penalty comes from without.
comments.comment: … the good is within us. For it is said: 'the kingdom of heaven is within you' (Luke 17:21). For we have a natural inclination toward the virtue which he has called 'kingdom'. But the penalty and the evil come from without, as does the shame of sin. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's question whether he will find faith on earth fits our times, when no one considers the day of the Lord or fears the punishments to come.
comments.comment: … And therefore the Lord, looking upon our times, says in his Gospel: "When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?" (Luke 18:8). We see happening what he foretold. There is no faith in the fear of God, in the law of justice, in love, in good work. No one thinks about the fear of things to come; no one considers the day of the Lord, the wrath of God, the punishments that are to come upon the unbelieving, and the eternal torments appointed for the faithless. Whatever our conscience would fear if it believed, it does not fear at all because it does not believe …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Lord's question about finding faith on earth.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: The question about finding faith on earth is said of us who are called Christians.
comments.comment: … About whom is the word, that 'When the Son of Man comes, will he find the faith on the earth?' (Luke 18:8) Is it not about us? For this reason let us attend to ourselves, doing everything, that day by day this flock of God may be improved, healed, cured, and every crushing depart from our souls …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Pharisee is condemned not for tithing but for condemning all humanity with his own word.
comments.comment: … He did not lie about these things, but even if it seemed to him to speak truths, he is condemned; not because he believed or tithed what was his, but because he condemned all humanity with his own word. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Pharisee was condemned though what he said was true.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: The tax collector went down justified, for those who exalt themselves will be humbled.
comments.comment: … But the tax collector, the sinner, beating his breast, the fountain of thoughts, not counting the entitlements of the belly like the Pharisee, nor even daring to lift his eyes to heaven, said: 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner' (Luke 18:13). To this the Lord said: 'Amen I say to you, that the tax collector descended justified rather than that Pharisee' (Luke 18:14). And so that no one might think these things were said to him regarding the two persons, he added, saying: 'For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted' (Luke 14:11). …
comments.selected_reason: Gives the tax collector's prayer and the Lord's verdict in plain terms.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Called good, the Lord sent the speaker back to his Father, who alone is good.
comments.comment: … Our Saviour and Lord, hearing himself once addressed as “Good Teacher” (Mark 10:17; Luke 18:18), sent the speaker back to his own Father and said: “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, God the Father” (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Lord's answer to 'Good Teacher'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hard saying about the rich can mean the man hindered by wealth as by thorns, or the man rich in false doctrines.
comments.comment: From these points too, then, it is clear how Jesus, the “Nazarene” man, does not lay down contrary laws [to those of Moses] in what he said about wealth and about those who were amazed, namely, that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God (Mark 10:23–26; Luke 18:24). This holds whether one takes the “rich man” more simply as the one who is distracted by wealth and hindered by it, as by thorns, from bearing the fruits of the word (Matthew 13:22), or as the one who is rich in false doctrines, of whom it is written in Proverbs: “Better a poor man who is righteous than a rich man who is a liar” …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the saying about the rich entering the kingdom may mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Family is to be left only when it drags toward impiety, so the wife is spoken of in a spiritual sense.
comments.comment: Luke has also added concerning a wife (Luke 18:29) — according to Paul, who commands to honor “elder women as mothers, younger as sisters in all purity.” (1 Timothy 5:2) Just as he gives brothers who are not brothers, parents who are not parents, and children who are not children, so also a wife who is not a wife, fulfilling the intimacies in another, clearly spiritual manner, not bodily. Leaving the race according to the flesh is good for the spiritual life; for he says to separate from parents and from a wife when they drag toward impiety. Just as one must despise soul and body for piety, so one must also prefer this to all things.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The crowd called him Jesus the Nazarene, but the blind man preached the truth by calling him Son of David.
comments.comment: … What, he asks, does the crowd intend? They say to him, "Jesus the Nazarene is passing by" (Luke 18:37). Oh, the wonder! Other things are being taught, and other things are being preached; he hears Jesus the Nazarene, but he does not call him Jesus the Nazarene, but Jesus the Son of David (Matthew 20:30). Those seeing from presumption were speaking, but the blind man was preaching from truth. "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (Matthew 20:30). …
comments.selected_reason: Shows the contrast between the crowd's words and the blind man's cry.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Jericho is named so that Zacchaeus, who welcomed Jesus, may be set beside Rahab, who welcomed Joshua.
comments.comment: The evangelist does not mention Jericho without purpose, but because he is speaking of a tax collector who welcomed God into his home. The matter was hard to believe. He sets his homeland before us, so that when we remember Rahab the prostitute we may not be shocked at the strange turning back of Zacchaeus. This is why he mentioned Jericho: so that, calling to mind Rahab the prostitute, we may compare the manner of salvation of both. For just as Rahab the prostitute received Joshua son of Nun as a spy and hid him, so Zacchaeus the tax collector received the true Jesus, who spies out our minds, into his home and nourished him. She received Joshua son of Nun, who led the people into the land of promise; this man receives the true Jesus, who leads into the kingdom of heaven. She received Joshua, who razed the temple of the Jews; this man received the true Jesus, who foretold that razing. For he says, “Not one stone will be left here upon another that will not be thrown down” (Matthew 24:2). She received Joshua, who led the people through the Jordan into a land flowing with milk and honey; this man received the true Jesus, who through baptism leads the faithful to what no eye has seen and no ear has heard and what has not entered the human heart (1 Corinthians 2:9). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse names Jericho, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Where Jesus is received as a guest everything changes for the better, so that the tax collector's house becomes a paradise.
comments.comment: "Hurry, then, and come down, for today I must stay in your house" (Luke 19:5). O grace beyond telling! O love for humanity beyond speech! The house that receives Jesus is cleansed. For wherever Jesus is received as guest, everything changes for the better. "Zacchaeus," he says, "hurry and come down, for today I must stay in your house." What can I say? The tax collector's house has become paradise. For what I see in the thief, I see also in Zacchaeus. He said to the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43), and taking him from the tree he brought him into paradise. He said to Zacchaeus, "Today I must stay in your house," and taking him he entered, making his house a paradise before paradise. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Jesus' words to Zacchaeus mean.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Zacchaeus gave to the poor before Christ had taught him anything, because the Savior's presence shone on him as the sun lights a house.
comments.comment: And see the wonderful thing: immediately Zacchaeus, standing before the door, says: 'Lord, I give half of my possessions to the poor' (Luke 19:8). You have not yet been taught, and you obey? You have not yet learned, and you have kept it? The Savior said nothing, nothing he taught, nothing about almsgiving he proposed, not love of the poor he commanded then, but he was silent, and by resting he enlightened; and just as a sun entering through the rays into a house, not by a word it enlightens, but by that energy it shines; so also the Savior, having entered, with the rays of righteousness cut off the path of injustice; 'For the light shines in the darkness' (John 1:5), as the evangelist says.
comments.selected_reason: Shows what moved Zacchaeus to give in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Those who would have Christ dwell in them must first wash away their offenses, as Zacchaeus promised to repay fourfold, for dye takes only in clean wool.
comments.comment: … So also Zacchaeus the tax collector, when called to apostleship, promised not only that he would follow the one who had called him, but also that he would give back fourfold whatever he had taken by wrong (Luke 19:8). For I think that those who are to make Christ dwell within themselves through the Spirit (Ephesians 3:16–17) must first wash off their filth and first scour away their offenses, and so show him their own soul bright and spotless, just as the divinely inspired Psalmist, having reached this fine state of virtue, cried aloud: ‘My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody’ (Psalm 57:7). For just as dyes settle into wool when it is clean, but if any trace of dirt remains, what was taken in is at once easily shed and finds no firm hold in it, so too participation in Christ sinks into holy and pure souls, but would not settle at all in those that are not so. ‘For the Holy Spirit of wisdom will flee from deceit,’ as it is written, ‘and will not dwell in a body in debt to sins’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4–5). So by making amends to those who have been wronged, and by good deeds that lead to friendship and shear away our brothers’ grief, we shall free ourselves from every charge and gain the forgiveness that is in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Christ is to be made a partner in our goods, and what is given to the poor is given to him, as Zacchaeus gave half.
comments.comment: Therefore it is necessary to attend to how one must make Christ a brother. Take him as a partner of your things. Do you not want to grant everything to him? Even if you give half, give it to him like Zacchaeus (Luke 19:8). For to him, he says, Zacchaeus gave, not to the poor. But listen: he who shows mercy to the poor lends to God (Proverbs 19:17). Giving to the poor, you have given to Christ (Matthew 25:40).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Christ would not accept Zacchaeus's gifts to the poor until he had undone his greed against those he had wronged, and then declared salvation had come.
comments.comment: … Remember the tax collector Zacchaeus, who resolved to repay fourfold whatever he had defrauded, and then distributed half of his remaining goods to the poor. For he knew that he wished to receive Christ, and Christ would not accept his generosity toward the poor unless the greed against those he had wronged was dissolved. And so the Lord accepted Zacchaeus’s uprightness and said, “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19:9). These words are for those who practice almsgiving but do not take thought for fairness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Zacchaeus repays before he gives.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Christ called Zacchaeus a son of Abraham only after he promised charity and repayment, which are the works of the patriarch.
comments.comment: The Savior, having received this voice, says: 'Today salvation has come to this house' (Luke 19:9). He justified himself, not because he simply saw Christ, but because he obeyed the laws of Christ. Today salvation has come to this house, because this man also is a son of Abraham. Before doing the works of Abraham, he does not call him a son of Abraham, but calls him Zacchaeus by the bare appellation; but when he fulfilled the works of the patriarch, promising charity and the restitution of the injustice, then he says: 'And this man also is a son of Abraham.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Zacchaeus is called a son of Abraham.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: The Lord was received by rich tax collectors and did not tell them to drop their money, but took away its unjust use and kept its just use.
comments.comment: … But the Lord himself is received as a guest by Zacchaeus and Levi and Matthew, rich persons and tax collectors, and he does not command them to let go of their money. Instead, he imposes the just use of it and takes away the unjust use, and he declares, "Today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9). He praises their use of money so much that he commands sharing with this addition: give drink to the thirsty, give bread to the hungry, take in the homeless, clothe the naked.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Lord asks of the rich in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: The Savior seeks the lost soul in order to lead it into salvation, and his disciples do the same by instruction and by contributing to the good.
comments.comment: … He who seeks to bring the sinning soul to repentance and guide the one who has strayed from the truth back to it., seeks the soul praiseworthily and profitably. For the Savior indeed 'has come to seek and to save the lost' (Luke 19:10). He, seeking the soul, seeks in order that he might lead it into salvation, so that he might restore it according to its former state. Just as therefore the Savior does this through instruction and through contributing to the good, so also the disciples and angels and men of the Savior do this. And none of these, seeking the soul, speaks vanity, and none seeks evils against it, but good and profitable things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Rewards will match each one's good deeds, as the Lord sets one servant over ten cities and another over five.
comments.comment: That the repayment of reward will be in proportion to each one’s good deeds, and that God will allot to those who have chosen to act nobly rewards matched to their labors, the Savior himself will assure us. He says that the talents were not handed out in equal shares (Matthew 25:15), and of those who did well he sets one over ten cities and another over five (Luke 19:17–19). For each one’s life is weighed, as it were, in the balance, and the repayment will surely be equal in weight to our goodness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the servants receive different rewards.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: The colt on which no one had sat is the nations, which the apostles untied from darkness and brought to the Lord who now reigns over them.
comments.comment: They were sent “to bring the colt to Him” (Luke 19:35), and the colt is the nations, so that He might mount them and reign over them, as the psalmist says: “God has become King over the nations; the Lord sits on His holy throne” (Psalm 47:8). “On which no one has ever sat” (Mark 11:2; Luke 19:30): for the nations had neither God mounting and ruling over them, nor law, nor prophets. “Untie it,” He says, “and bring it to Me” (Matthew 21:2; Luke 19:30). For the apostles untied the nations from darkness, that is, from ignorance of God; from error, from sin, from slavery to an alien master, from “the power of darkness” (Colossians 1:13), from “the ruler of this age” (John 12:31). And they brought them to the Lord, their Creator and Maker.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The garments on the colt signify the grace given to the nations and also their own virtues, which they joined to grace.
comments.comment: “And they put the garments on the colt” (Matthew 21:7): these signify the grace He gave them among the nations, and through this grace “they set Jesus on them” (Luke 19:35). And not only through grace, but also through their own virtues, as the evangelist signifies when he says: “And others spread their garments on the road” (Luke 19:36). By this he hints at their own virtues, which they yoked to grace, as the inspired Paul says plainly: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we boast in hope of the glory of God” (Romans 5:1–2).
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: The angels had peace among themselves in heaven, but not peace with human beings, so that heaven kept its peace to itself.
comments.comment: And see, He sits on them and reigns as upon the cherubim (Psalm 99:1), while they cry out and say: “Hosanna in the highest, blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Matthew 21:9; Luke 19:38), for so Luke puts it. Why does he say, “Peace in heaven”? Did the angels not have peace in heaven? Yes, they certainly had peace among themselves, “the peace that surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7), as the most wise Paul says. They had peace in heaven, but they did not have it with human beings; heaven, then, kept its peace to itself. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the crowd cries 'peace in heaven.'
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: On Lazarus and the Palm Branches

comments.capsule: Christ answered the Sadducees that in the resurrection there is no marriage, since marriage was instituted to make up death's losses.
comments.comment: He [Christ] answered: ‘You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor God’s power (Matthew 22:29). In the resurrection they neither marry nor take wives, for they will not die’ (Matthew 22:29–30; Luke 20:35–36). Knowing his own work, he explained why he had instituted marriage: reproduction would make up death’s losses. Generous fertility would cease at once when grasping death ceased.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Christ's answer about marriage in the resurrection.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Human beings, once made perfect, become equal to angels, and have hope of rising to a likeness with the heavenly ranks and finally with God.
comments.comment: We know also that the angels are so far above human beings that human beings, once made perfect, become equal to angels; for “in the resurrection of the dead” the righteous “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of heaven” (Matthew 22:30; compare Mark 12:25), and they become “equal to angels” (Luke 20:36). We know that in the ordering of the universe there are some who are called thrones, others dominions, others authorities and others rulers (Colossians 1:16). And we see that we human beings, though we fall far short of these, have hope that by living well and doing everything in accordance with reason we shall rise to a likeness with all of them. And lastly, since “it has not yet been revealed what we shall be, we know that when he is revealed we shall be like God and shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'equal to angels' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The poor woman who gave the least, but all she had, carried off the testimony of giving more, because the sacred word weighs the giver's intention, not the amount.
comments.comment: … So it is recorded in the sacred books that a small and poor woman, among the rich and powerful who were offering great and costly gifts from their wealth, contributed small things, the very least, yet all that she had, and she alone carried off the testimony of having given more (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4). For I think the sacred word did not weigh generosity and magnificence by the amount of the material given, which is outside a person, but by the intention of the one offering it, or rather by the choice.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the widow's small gift counts for more.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Christ admired the widow's small and cheap gift, which may be great to those in the deepest poverty.
comments.comment: … Christ, of course, did not leave without admiration the widow in Jerusalem who brought to the treasury something small and very easy to come by (Mark 12:41–44; Luke 21:1–4), yet perhaps great for those in the deepest poverty, for whom even parting with the cheapest things is likely to be a hardship.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: Christ set aside the talk of the temple's adornments and foretold its fall to the Roman army, and the disciples then asked when it would be.
comments.comment: Some were showing Christ the great works in the temple and the adornment of the offerings; for they supposed he would marvel with them at what was seen — though he is God and has heaven as his throne. He sets aside talk about those things, but has foretold that it will fall from its foundations in due times, when the Roman army brings it to that end and all Jerusalem exacts from Israel the penalties for killing the Lord. For after the Savior’s cross these things happened to them to suffer, yet they did not understand the force of what was said. They supposed he was weaving words about the completion of the age. So they asked when these things would be, and what the sign would be when it was about to happen (Luke 21:7).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus foretold the armies around Jerusalem while the city still stood, and armies did not surround it until Nero's reign.
comments.comment: … while Jerusalem still stood and the whole Jewish worship was carried on in it, Jesus foretold what would befall it at the hands of the Romans. … Now it is written in them [the Gospels]: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near” (Luke 21:20). At that time there were no armies at all around Jerusalem, encircling it, enclosing it and besieging it. That began while Nero was still emperor and went on until the reign of Vespasian, whose son Titus destroyed Jerusalem …
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the verse was fulfilled.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even if heaven and earth pass away, the 'words,' the principles of each thing, will never pass away, as the Lord said.
comments.comment: … For we know that even if “heaven and earth” pass away, and the things in them, still the “words,” the principles of each thing, which stand to the Word who was “in the beginning” “with God,” God the Word (John 1:1), as parts to a whole or species to a genus, will never pass away. For we choose to listen to him who said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away” (Matthew 24:35; Mark 13:31; Luke 21:33).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ will not eat the Passover until it is fulfilled, out of pity for the disciples, preferring to become himself the Passover, whose name means a surpassing.
comments.comment: … for Luke says: 'When it became hour, he sat down, and the twelve apostles with him. And he said to them: With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer; for I say to you, I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God' (Luke 22:14-18). For he did not say again 'I shall not eat it,' but 'I shall not eat,' indicating his sympathy toward the disciples, because he pitied them, as they were going to have the feast unobserved due to his departure; for this is the 'I desired to eat the Passover with you before I suffer,' bringing forth that they shall have sorrow, and he will prefer, over their cheerfulness, that which is profitable to both them and the whole world—not to eat the Passover, but to become himself a Passover, whose fulfillment is 'in the kingdom of God,' when it completely surpasses death; for this is what the word Passover indicates, signifying a surpassing.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: At the table we eat and drink to remember always the one who died and rose for us, and we are told to discern the Lord's body, approaching with flesh and spirit cleansed.
comments.comment:
… “So Jesus took bread, and having given thanks, he broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said: Take, eat; this is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in remembrance of me. And he took the cup, and having given thanks, he gave it to them, saying: Drink from it, all of you. For this is my blood of the New Covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Luke 22:19-20). And the Apostle says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:26). What then are these words, and what benefit comes from them? It is so that, as we eat and drink, we may always remember the one who died and rose for us, and so be necessarily taught to keep that apostolic commandment given to us, which says: “For the love of Christ constrains us, because we have judged this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14-15). For the one who eats and drinks clearly does so for an indelible remembrance of the obedience unto death of the Master and Creator, who for my sake became what the formed thing was.

But we are not commanded to eat simply; rather, we are urged to discern this body of the Lord—clearly, having put away defilement of flesh and spirit, and having prepared a vessel for the spiritual ointment, so to approach the pure sacrifice …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Lord's words at the supper are for.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Christ honors the servant's place because of his humanity, yet remains the Master, served by all creation as God.
comments.comment: …in the Master’s way he almost shakes off being thought of in a servant’s rank; yet he honors this [rank] because of the human [nature he took]. “For I am,” he says, “in your midst as the one who serves.” (Luke 22:27) So even if he has come down among servants, he is still himself the one reclining — as Master, and served by all creation as God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ can say he serves while still being Master.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Luke records Christ announcing the coming war by telling the disciples to buy a sword; he forgave their use of it, then stopped any further use.
comments.comment: It also seems there was a forgiveness from the Lord regarding their use of the sword then [at his arrest]. For Luke recorded this as the Savior manifesting the impending war by saying, 'let someone sell his garment and buy a sword' (Luke 22:36), while the disciples said, 'look, two swords are here' (Luke 22:38), to which he replied, 'it is enough' (Luke 22:38). This was not a mindless thing being forgiven by the Lord, who commanded not to resist 'the evil one,' but also for the sake of what was said, so that he might show by deed what he had foretold by word, and since they were using the righteous sword, he stood and prevented them, so that they would no longer use it; as he himself, having said these things, recorded that after saying this, the Lord said, 'let it be until this,' and this 'until' has a limit and a prohibition of the use of the sword according to the law.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ's being treated as a criminal was foretold: God was numbered with the lawless when men chose a robber and crucified Jesus between two robbers.
comments.comment: Second, we say [in answer to the charge that Jesus was like a robber] that even these things were in some way foretold in the Gospels, since God “was numbered with the lawless” (Luke 22:37; Isaiah 53:12) in the judgment of lawless men, who wanted rather a robber released, the one who had been thrown into prison “for sedition” “and murder” (Luke 23:18–19; John 18:40), and Jesus crucified, and who crucified him between two robbers (Matthew 27:38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'numbered with the lawless' meant in the events of the passion.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the Son of Man sits at the right hand of God's power, sharing the Father's throne, Christ is God, for a created nature does not sit with the God who is so by nature.
comments.comment: So Christ said to them — clearly to the chief priests of the Jews who were asking: “If you are the Christ, tell us. If I tell you, you will not believe; and if I ask, you will not answer. But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” (Luke 22:67–69) If the Son of Man sits at the right hand of God’s power, how is Christ not God — shining in the highest seats and sharing the Father’s throne? For a created nature does not sit with the God who is so by nature at all; yet the Son of Man does sit with him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says about where the Son of Man sits.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: The moist tree stands for the righteous man and the dry for the impious, and Christ is the true righteous tree, who shared the world's misfortunes without sin, as righteous people do.
comments.comment: … "Behold, I kindle a fire in you, and it will consume every tree in you"—Aquila says "moist"; the Septuagint, "and every dry tree" (Ezekiel 20:47). The moist tree is an allegory for the righteous man, and the dry tree for the impious. The Lord himself showed that he is the true righteous tree when he said, "If they do these things when the wood is moist, what will happen when it is dry?" (Luke 23:31). And if the Lord shared in the misfortunes brought upon the world insofar as he shared in flesh, though he had no sin, it is no wonder that righteous human beings, who are in some way partakers of sin, also become partakers of the misfortunes that follow upon sins. They suffer equally with the unjust, being put to death just as he himself was counted among the lawless, yet they are distinguished before God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the moist and dry wood in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Christ prayed for those crucifying him, answering evil with goodness and dissolving the charge by attributing it to ignorance.
comments.comment: And while suffering these things, he prayed for those who were crucifying him, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34). He conquers evil with goodness. He speaks in defense of those who killed Christ, saving them. He dissolves the charge by attributing it to ignorance. He is not angry at becoming the plaything of their drunken violence. He accepts the drunkenness and in love for humanity calls them to repentance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ asks forgiveness for those who know not what they do.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: Of the two robbers, one shared the Jews' hostility, while the other believed, rebuked them, confessed his sin and called the dying Christ king.
comments.comment: One of the robbers, sharing the Jews’ lovelessness toward God, belched out the same words as they: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” (Luke 23:39) But the other, walking the opposite road, is fittingly marvelled at. He has believed in him though hung in so bitter a punishment; he rebukes the Jews’ loose-mouthedness and the co-hung man’s voices; he confessed the sin so that he might appear more just. For he bore witness that Christ was wholly without blame and was an accuser of the crucifiers’ madness; and so he seized the lot of the holy — the enrollment above and in the heavens. Seeing him crucified, he was calling him king; he expected the one in dishonor and suffering to come in God-befitting glory; he seized the faith though not raised in nobility — and he also benefits us, opening the heavens to us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Peter, Paul, Abraham and Isaiah believed on seeing glory, but the robber cried out to Christ though he saw him only in insolence.
comments.comment: Peter believed, but seeing the dead raised and beholding his glory, he believed; Paul believed, but seeing light from heaven, which scorched the bodily eyes and enlightened the spiritual eyes; Abraham believed, but beholding a divine vision; Isaiah believed, but seeing him sitting upon a high throne and the Cherubim around him. All saw, but in glory; but this one in insolence; therefore he also cried out, 'Remember me, Lord, when you come in your kingdom' (Luke 23:42).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A single assent of faith brought the thief into paradise.
comments.comment: For what does he say? 'Remember me, Lord, in your kingdom' (Luke 23:42). And by a single assent of faith he dwells in paradise and walks about the heavens. 'For truly I say to you,' he says, 'today you will be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the thief received so great a promise.
comments.author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
comments.work: Homily I on the Holy Pascha

comments.capsule: The crowds returned striking their breasts, and the Lord lifted on the cross drew the centurion and some of the Jews, as he had said he would.
comments.comment: And the crowds who had come to the spectacle were returning, striking their breasts — freeing themselves, perhaps, from impiety against Christ by crying out against the crucifiers, even if not openly, because of the leaders’ unholiness. So great was the power of the one being crucified — this centurion afterward proving steadfast in the faith (Matthew 27:54). The Lord was speaking truly when he said, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself.” (John 12:32) For look: lifted on the precious cross, he began to net many into knowledge of the truth. He drew the centurion, and he also drew some of the Jews, who were striking their breasts, pricked in mind and looking up toward the Lord with the eyes of understanding (Luke 23:48).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the crowd's grief at the cross as the Lord drawing people to himself.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The evangelists took care to record that the tomb was hewn in rock and that no one had yet lain there, which is worth reflecting on.
comments.comment: … For now it is enough to mention the clean linen cloth in which the pure body of Jesus had to be wrapped (Matthew 27:59), and the new tomb “which” Joseph “had hewn in the rock” (Matthew 27:60), “where no one had yet lain” (Luke 23:53), or, as John says, “in which no one had yet been placed” (John 19:41). Consider whether the agreement of the three evangelists can move anyone. They took care to record that the tomb was quarried or hewn in rock (Matthew 27:60; Mark 15:46; Luke 23:53), so that whoever examines the meaning of what is written may see something worth reflecting on about these things too, and about the newness of the tomb, which Matthew and John relate, and about no dead body having been there, as Luke and John say.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Matthew and Mark speak of the one angel who rolled away the stone, while Luke and John speak of the two who stood by the women, so the accounts do not contradict.
comments.comment: He [Celsus] did not notice, I think, that Matthew and Mark reported one (Matthew 28:2–5; Mark 16:5), and Luke and John two (Luke 24:4; John 20:12). These accounts were not contradictory. For those who recorded one say that this was the one who rolled away “the stone” from the tomb (Matthew 28:2); while the others say that the two are those who, “in dazzling clothing” (Luke 24:4), stood by the women who had come to the tomb, or those who were seen inside “sitting in white” (John 20:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Gospels speak of one angel or two.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jesus, of a more divine nature, could become invisible whenever he wished, as Luke shows when he vanished from the two after breaking bread.
comments.comment: … that it was not impossible for him, as one of a more divine nature, to become invisible whenever he wished, is clear in itself. It is plain also from what is written about him, to anyone except those who accept some of the writings in order to attack the word, and think others are fictions. Now it is written in the Gospel according to Luke that after the resurrection Jesus “took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it” to Simon and Cleopas; and when they had taken the bread, “their eyes were opened, and they recognised him; and he vanished from their sight” (Luke 24:30–31).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jesus vanished at the breaking of bread.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If the Gospels had said he vanished from the cross at once, unbelievers would have objected anyway, so his choosing when to vanish should lead them to believe in the resurrection.
comments.comment: Moreover, suppose it had been written in the Gospels that he vanished from the stake at once: Celsus and the unbelievers would have found fault with what was written, and would have brought a charge in this form too, saying: “Why ever did he vanish after the cross, and not contrive this before he suffered?” If, then, having learned from the Gospels that he did not vanish from the stake at once, they think they can find fault with the account for not inventing, as they demanded, that he vanished from the stake at once, but for relating the truth, is it not reasonable that they should also believe in his resurrection? And should they not believe that when he chose, at one time, “the doors being shut,” he “stood in the midst” of the disciples (John 20:19, 26), and at another, having given bread to two of his followers, at once “vanished from their sight” (Luke 24:31), after speaking certain words to them?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The burning of the heart on the Emmaus road is to be praised, because this fire acts, as heat reshapes gold or silver into a vessel, rather than harming as it does wood.
comments.comment: And the meditation and the heat of the Holy Spirit is the all-consuming, which comes to pass by the blowing Spirit. Therefore the fire burns in order that it may act, not in order that it may harm and consume. 'Was not our heart burning within us while he opened to us the Scriptures?' (Lk 24:32). This burning is to be praised. And observe also regarding manufactured things: some are heated in order that they may be reshaped and become a vessel, gold or silver. But if wood or something else is set on fire, the heat is harmful.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ had them handle him, and ate and showed his wounds, to prove his body was real, not an appearance.
comments.comment: Since entering with the doors shut he made the disciples doubt whether perhaps what appeared was not a body but only a type, Luke clarifying the mind said: “Handle me and see, that a spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39) and he ate and showed the flesh’s wounds.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ says 'handle me and see.'
comments.author: Ammonius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord opened the disciples' minds, and understanding drives away deception.
comments.comment: The oracles need to be opened. Therefore the Lord opened the mind of the disciples to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45), and the understanding given through the words drives away the deception that comes through pleasure or glory (Psalm 119:130; LXX 118:130).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea
